speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. G. F. Higgins (St. John's East):
subtopic: INQUIRY WITH RESPECT TO DEATH OF CANADIAN CIVILIAN
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Was the recent death of a Canadian civilian at Goose Bay airport caused by his being fired at by a United States sentry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: INQUIRY WITH RESPECT TO DEATH OF CANADIAN CIVILIAN
speechtext:
I have not the file on this case, as the intimation that the hon. gentleman was to ask the question reached me only a few minutes before I came into the house. My recollection of the events is that on April 27, at about eleven p.m., two civilian employees of a contractor were driving in a jeep and had an altercation with some United States army men at one of the mess halls occupied by them. In the course of driving the jeep, the civilians were alleged to have driven to the danger of a United States policeman, who shot at the jeep with his revolver with, as he said, the intention of stopping but not hitting the men. They drove on at a high rate of speed and he pursued them. In the course of the pursuit the civilian jeep was overturned and the passenger killed, although the driver was not injured. Neither was hit by the revolver fire of the United States policeman.
The accident was at once investigated oh the spot by Canadian and United States officials, including the R.C.M.P. acting for the Newfoundland provincial government. A charge of drunken driving was laid against the civilian driver. We sent from headquarters an R.C.A.F. officer from the judge

advocate general's branch to make an investigation. The matter is now pending before the courts. So far as can be seen, it is largely a matter which should be handled by the authorities of the government of Newfoundland.

Mr. Speaker, first I should like to thank the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond for bringing this matter to my attention. The officers of the department investigated the news item to which the hon. member refers, and found that no such parade was organized in Vancouver. With regard to the complaint that no provision for unemployment insurance benefits has been made for veterans discharged from the Korean forces, may I say that that is not according to the facts. By virtue of the authority granted under the special forces act passed last session, an order in council was passed on November 8 which gave unemployment insurance benefits to all veterans who have served for three months. Any veteran of the Canadian Army special force in Korea must have served a minimum of three months.
With regard to the clothing allowance, the hon. member will recall that at the end of the last war this was paid by the Department of National Defence and was included with the last pay cheque given to the man on discharge. This is one of the questions under study by the interdepartmental committee which is now looking into the question of veterans benefits.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since the beginning of the session a number of statements have been made on matters relating to defence, and for the convenience of hon. members I should like to give references to them. The statements were announced by me except in the cases noted. They were made on February 5, as reported at page 90 of Hansard, on the defence program; there was a statement by the Minister of Defence Production on February 8, at page 179 of Hansard; another statement by myself on February 21, 1951, at page 563 of Hansard, on the brigade group joining the Princess Patricias; a statement by the Prime Minister on March 9, 1951, at page 1077 of Hansard, on the Defence Production Act; by myself

Supply-National Defence on March 21, 1951, at page 1485 of Hansard, on the air training plan; by myself on April 19, 1951, at page 2173 of Hansard, on the bombing and gunnery range; by myself on April 24, 1951, at page 2317 of Hansard, on the recruiting of women; by the Prime Minister on May 1, 1951, at page 2549 of Hansard, on the arrangements in connection with the Newfoundland bases; by me on May 1, 1951, at page 2553 of Hansard, on the formation of the commonwealth division; by the Minister of Veterans Affairs on May 1, 1951, at page 2554 of Hansard, on the extension of benefits to veterans; on May 4, 1951, at page 2703 of Hansard, on the formation of the 27th Canadian infantry brigade.
In addition, yesterday we tabled the white paper, "Canada's Defence Program," incorporating a good deal of this material and giving other information about defence in very considerable detail. Consequently I do not feel that it is necessary or desirable for me to make a very comprehensive and detailed statement at this time. However, there are some matters of great importance about which I feel hon. members would wish me to say something at the outset, and also some matters which have come up since the white paper was prepared.
The object of all defence policy, Mr. Chairman, is to preserve the security of our country. It is better to prevent a war than to have to fight a war to victory. Our primary responsibility is the defence of our country against direct attack. All Canadians realize, I believe, that the best place to defend Canada is as far away from our shores as possible; but they also recognize that we cannot do it alone, that we must have allies with whom we plan and work, and, if need be, fight in close co-operation shoulder to shoulder; that the only possible aggressor would be imperialist communism working under one guise or another; that the object of our defence activities is to prevent war by providing the force to deter aggression or, if necessary, to stop aggression should it occur; that our defence activities do not constitute an end in themselves but a means toward providing the strength which will prevent aggression and prevent war so that the human and material resources of our nation, and of all other nations, can be used to extend the areas of human freedom and increase the level of family and individual prosperity and happiness.
So far as we can, during this period we must continue to strengthen the democracy which is the object as well as one of the main bulwarks of our defence. We must also continue to do everything we can to improve the level of our society, raise the standard of
[Mr. Claxton.1
living and enlarge freedom and opportunity throughout our country. We must not lose either our democratic methods or our democratic objectives without fighting a battle. In this the record of Canada and of other countries has shown that we can do a good job, and that victory will be ours with peace, or, if it should come, with war; but the greater victory will be without war.
Developments in international affairs, particularly over the last two years, have reinforced the concept that in the defence of Canada we must work with other countries. In this connection I should like to refer to the developments in Korea, our part in the operations there, and to the organization established under the North Atlantic treaty.
On June 25, 1950, the North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel. The following day, on the initiative of the United States government, the security council of the United Nations adopted a declaration condemning this as an act of unprovoked aggression and calling on members of the United Nations to suppress this aggressive action by sea and air action. From its forces in the Far East the United States put into action several naval vessels and a squadron of the air force two days later.
It became apparent that the aggressors would not be stopped by sea and air forces alone, and on July 2 the United States put in ground forces. On July 7 the security council recommended that other nations make military forces and other assistance available to the unified command under the United States, and requested the United States to designate the commander. General MacArthur was designated as commander. Other nations having forces in the Far East were the United Kingdom and Australia. On July 26, 1950, the United Kingdom made available one brigade, while Australia sent a regiment from Japan, later reinforced with other troops. Other nations which have taken part are Belgium, France, Greece, India, New Zealand, the Netherlands, the Philippines, Turkey, Thailand and Colombia.
We sent three destroyers on July 5, made available a heavy air transport squadron on July 19, and the same day arranged for additional air transport through Canadian Pacific Air Lines. On July 20 we announced a greatly expanded defence program. On August 7 we announced the formation, and two days later began the recruiting of a special force which, with elements of the regular forces, was to be made available to the unified command. Recruiting was speeded and training pressed on so that the 25th Canadian infantry brigade

Group had completed basic and advanced individual training and special unit training by the time it arrived at Fort Lewis in the state of Washington between November 16 and November 23. It made a fine impression on its first parade which I was privileged to witness.
At this stage the manner of employing our brigade group was entirely dependent on the development of events. On November 4, 1950, it had been announced that the Princess Patricias would proceed to Korea, and they left on November 25. The rest of the brigade group continued to complete its training at Fort Lewis. On March 28 an advance party of the brigade proceeded to Korea, and Brigadier Rockingham, its commander, also went out to see conditions in Korea, and to make arrangements for the arrival of the brigade.
Returning to events in Korea, by August 1, 1950, the North Korean forces had succeeded in driving back the United Nations forces to a limited beachhead in the Pusan area. During the next six weeks the United Nations forces achieved a build-up which enabled them on September 15, 1950, to launch a counteroffensive. This offensive resulted in the virtual destruction of the North Korean army, and by October 28, 1950, the United Nations forces had driven to within forty miles of the Manchurian border. On November 30 the Chinese communist forces intervened and the United Nations advance was halted. The enemy's offensive operations had by January 1, 1951, forced the withdrawal of the United Nations forces to the vicinity of the 37th parallel. Then the communist attack lost its momentum due to extended lines of communication, inadequate air support, large casualties, particularly those due to sickness, and their inability to cope with cold weather conditions, as well as the increased fighting strength of the United Nations.
On January 25, 1951, the United Nations forces resumed the offensive and advanced steadily through February and March until by April 21, 1951, they had reached a general line immediately north of the 38th parallel. Meanwhile the enemy had succeeded in concentrating a mass of manpower and material in the immediate battle area. On April 22 the present enemy counter-offensive was launched with an estimated 350,000 men representing about half the total enemy forces in Korea. At present the United Nations forces in western Korea are occupying defensive positions along a general line approximately five miles north of Seoul, and at the moment the position has been stabilized. Total United
Supply-National Defence Nations forces in Korea, apart from the South Koreans, are estimated to be approximately
260,000.	We have 6,100 in the brigade group and 1,100 reinforcements in Korea in addition to those in Canada. Altogether we have trained reinforcements estimated to be sufficient for six months, with more being added day by day from current recruiting.
Turning to the question of casualties, estimates of enemy casualties are apt to be very far off the mark and usually exaggerated. One estimate is that over 800,000 casualties have been inflicted on the combined forces of the Chinese communists and North Koreans. During the same period United States casualties are reported to be 62,000, including 10,400 killed, 40,600 wounded and 11,000 missing. We have not the figures of the casualties suffered by the other United Nations forces. Our own Princess Patricias entered into action on February 22. Up to May 3 they had suffered 33 killed and 85 wounded. We mourn their loss, just as we deplore and regret that it should be necessary. All three services, navy, army and air force, are now making a substantial contribution to defeat aggression in North Korea. There I believe the magnitude of our effort is third among the United Nations co-operating in this work.
In the navy, army and air force we have a total of 8,337 officers and men involved in our operations in the Far East. This is in addition to men in the replacement group, supply lines, training establishments, and others. Of these 2,567 are in the active forces, and there are 5,770 who joined the Canadian Army special force.
The chief of the naval staff has handed me a letter he received from the officer commanding the forces with which our ships are serving in the Far East, which I think the house might be interested in hearing. It is dated March 29, 1951, and reads:
Dear Grant:
Now that HMCS Cayuga has left us, I wish to take the opportunity of her departure to tell you how extremely well the Canadian ships have done out here.
I sent you a copy of a letter I wrote to Taylor of the Sioux, and I find it hard to choose between any of the three we know so well, Sioux, Athabascan or Cayuga. The new arrivals, Nootka and Huron, will, I know, soon get worked in and play as big a part as their predecessors-they can't do more.
I should interpolate that since this letter was written the Sioux has arrived to replace the Athabaskan.
As for Brock-

Supply-National Defence
That is Captain Brock.
-he has handled his own ship and all your three ships (and for that matter any others that from time to time have been under him) very well. He has shown courage and common sense. His well-judged night entry into Chinnampo in early December was a fine bit of work.
I feel that he deserves my praise, and so do all the ships that you have sent us. They have set a high standard, and I am sure you have every reason to be proud of them and satisfied with their work.
This letter is signed by Vice Admiral William Andrewes, C.B., C.B.E., D.S.O.
The Princess Patricias have lived up to the splendid record of that fine regiment. I have seen the brigade twice, once when it first arrived at Fort Lewis and then just before they left. The views expressed by His Excellency the Governor General, who took the salute and inspected them that day, and by other distinguished' soldiers with wide experience and great records, confirm my impression that this brigade is one of which we may well be proud-tough, well trained, and well led.
The United States air force officers in command of McChord field, from which 426 squadron is operating its airlift, gave me exactly the same report about the R.C.A.F. I do not suppose it is generally recognized that on a round trip these twelve North Stars, flying west on the great circle route past the Aleutians, east by way of Honolulu, in order to take advantage of the weather and also to provide more comfortable service for the wounded they frequently carry back, travelling through most difficult weather and over some of the longest legs in the world, fly over 13,000 miles on each trip.
This is a fight, Mr. Speaker, in which international police action is working to stop communist aggression, communist gangsters. The forces of the United Nations for the first time are working and fighting shoulder to shoulder to stop aggression in Korea, and to show that aggression does not pay there or anywhere else. It is a magnificent thing that young Canadians should have volunteered to serve in such a cause. In taking the action we have, in co-operating in this way, I believe the great bulk of the Canadian people feel that we have done right. I believe they also feel that the government, the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have been right in doing everything possible to reduce the risks of a general war. The object of the effort in which we are participating is to show that aggression does not pay, to restore peaceful conditions in Korea and, by preventing aggression there, to preserve peace everywhere.
In this connection I should like to make it just as plain as I can that I profoundly disagree with the views expressed' on this subject in the house last evening by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). I am glad to say that they are not the views of this government. Moreover I do not believe any government holding those views would continue to have the support of the Canadian people. Certainly they do not express the objectives for which we are asking our young Canadians to serve gallantly a great cause far from home. Moreover, I believe-and I think all fifteen governments participating in the Far East have the same view-that were the views expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra to be adopted they would increase the risks of a general war, without increasing the opportunity for bringing about a successful termination of hostilities in Korea upon terms which would be acceptable to those nations.
You had better read it again.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
It would be interesting to learn whether the views expressed by this senior member of the Conservative opposition correctly express the views of that party or of any other considerable number of the members in this house.
Now, sir, may I turn to the North Atlantic treaty organization. References have been made before to our substantial contributions of equipment to the North Atlantic treaty nations. It is not expected we shall be making further deliveries of existing equipment until deliveries of substantial quantities of replacement equipment are forthcoming from the United States, or being produced here. We are also getting on with the training of aircrew for the countries participating. The first wings parade of navigators took place at Summerside last Friday, and it was a thrilling sight to see the young men coming up to take their wings behind the colours of the countries for which they are working, and the countries which are also working with us. In this case it was Belgium, Italy and Norway. Next week it will be France, and so on with all the countries that are taking advantage of our air training plan. It was a thrill for Canadians to see these men, called to receive the R.C.A.F. wing, proud because of the high standard of achievement our airmen have won for the wings of the R.C.A.F. in every corner of the world.
Reference has been made to the reopening of the airfields, and the acquisition of aircraft to look after this flow which we expect will build up to a total of about 3,300 R.C.A.F.

and NATO student fliers this year. A good many hon. members saw the F-86E fly at Toronto two weeks ago last Friday. This is the first Sabre to be equipped with our Canadian designed and made Orenda engine, with power perhaps greater than any jet engine being made. This increased the performance of the aircraft even over that which had previously made it the fastest fighter yet known. That afternoon this plane had completed a flight from Minneapolis to Toronto, a distance of 715 miles, in one hour and five minutes, or about 700 miles per hour, and that must be a record of some kind.
Yesterday we began to raise the 27th infantry brigade on the basis of the reserve force units. The reserve army units designated have taken hold of the job in a most creditable fashion. In Winnipeg yesterday I visited one of the depots and found that the procedure was working well. Shortly after ten o'clock the first recruit was completely examined, documented and in uniform. The reports which were received by defence headquarters this morning, which are still incomplete, indicate that a total of approximately 1,200 applications were received yesterday. This is regarded as a good response on the first day. It indicates that with the strong support of the reserve forces, and of the people of Canada, we should raise a force of considerable size which will be useful in meeting the responsibility ahead of us.
Many of the reserve units which have not been designated, while expressing proper and creditable regret, offered their hearty support in canvassing their men to join up during the plan. As seems to be almost inevitable in an operation of this kind, there were reports in the press which were entirely without foundation. One was to the effect that we were going light on Ottawa so as to keep the civil servants in their positions. There is absolutely no foundation whatever for that statement. Moreover, it was not made by any responsible officer at national defence headquarters. Then, there was another report, heard over the regional news in Ontario this morning, that while recruiting was going well in Montreal the response was largely from French-speaking applicants. This is the reverse of the usual suggestion, and on that account perhaps we should welcome it. But I venture to say that when the figures are checked it will be found that the English-speaking people of Montreal have responded to this as to every other appeal as well or better than their Englishspeaking friends in other parts of Canada.
Personally I deprecate beyond words these efforts to put one race against another in this or any other country. For this reason
Supply-National Defence among others we have not kept figures showing the racial origins of Canadians joining the armed forces. We regard them ail as Canadians. When questions of that type are asked or assertions made, they are not made for the purpose of maintaining national unity but for the very opposite.
However, in this connection I am going to break my own rule, a rule which has been observed by my predecessors and welcomed by the house. I do that because of two charges against French-speaking Canadians which are utterly and completely without foundation. I do that because they have been made in important publications in other countries. I refer first to an article on Canada's foreign policy in the Contemporary Review of February, 1951, published in England, by J. A. Stevenson, who said:
. . the comparatively small contingent of French Canadians, who have volunteered for the special UN force, indicates that the isolationist spirit still has a firm grip on the French-Canadian people.
In a similar article in Foreign Affairs published in the United States for April, 1951, the same author said:
The recruiting returns for the special United Nations forces showed a smaller proportion of volunteers from Quebec than from any other province.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in the interests of unity and justice, it is necessary to deny emphatically these unfortunate and inaccurate statements. It happens that we do keep figures of enlistments by districts and areas which generally correspond to the provincial boundaries. The total number of men enlisting in the special force was 10,587. Of those, 3,134 came from the province of Quebec, or thirty per cent. The inhabitants of the province of Quebec represent twenty-nine per cent of the population. In other words, far from the province of Quebec doing worse than the rest of the country, it did just about the same as the rest of the country, or a little better.
Moreover, I have had a special survey carried out. It meant looking at every file, but I thought in the interests of national unity and justice we should do it. It was found that the proportion of Canadians in all parts of the country who joined the special force and whose mother tongue was reported to be French corresponds almost exactly to the Canadians of French origin in the total population. I must say that when I was out there I saw the 22nd, the Princess Patricias and the Royal Canadian Regiment working as a single team. They had the utmost confidence in each other, as well they may have. They got on well. I believe that, just as in Italy and in western Europe, the forces of the two main streams of our culture and

Supply-National Defence of our country will be united in battle as in peace, more than ever before in the history of our country.
Now I should like to make it plain how the sixteen battalions were selected to form part of this brigade. There are over sixty infantry regiments in Canada. When we wanted to raise three battalions to constitute the 27th infantry brigade, plus some more to act as replacements or to rotate later, we were faced with the task either of choosing three battalions within the more than sixty or of dividing up the job and choosing, say, six or fifteen or some other number. We arrived at the fifteen in order to give a broad basis of geographical distribution and representation through all parts of the country.
Five companies are required for each battalion, and we wanted to have each of those five companies have something in common on which they would begin to build on the traditions of their particular type of unit; so we designated one battalion as a Canadian highland battalion, and to make up that battalion we asked five reserve Scottish regiments, from different parts of the country, each to send a company first and then another one later. Then we asked five rifle regiments and five line regiments to do the same thing. In this way it seemed to us that we were arriving at the double purpose of gaining the greatest possible support through tying in with the greatest number of units, and yet making the most of existing tradition, and thus form a battalion out of which a good commanding officer could fairly soon make a fine unit.
This plan was put up to the general officers commanding districts and then to the representatives of the defence associations representing the fourteen corps of reserve army units of non-regular soldiers. No objection was made to it. The G.O.C.'s, knowing the units in the districts, felt that this was the best way to do it. The reserve army representatives felt that this was a good thing to do, and they had no comment to make on the selection that had been made. I may say that it was made by the chief of the general staff and by the officers advising him; but it was discussed in detail by myself and approved by myself.
In selecting localities we had also to consider not only geographical distribution, not only the division into Scottish, line and infantry regiments but also the other types of regiments and units that we wanted to raise in each locality-artillery, engineers,


army service, intelligence corps, provost corps and so on. If, for instance, London, Ontario, had a good reserve army provost corps-and there are few of them in the reserve forces -it was designated as the place to raise the provost corps; and so on with the artillery and engineers, each contributing a battery or a troop, whatever might be appropriate, to form the unit. In the case of the armour- because this force is to be equipped with the latest type of tanks on which only, so far, officers and men of the permanent force have been fully trained-we decided to send the R.C.D.'s to supply replacements for a number of armoured regiments. The way in which it has been received seems to indicate that this plan, announced on Friday, put into effect over the week end and begun yesterday will do the job we set out to do provided it has strong and sustained support.
Further, it is the kind of thing that the reserve forces are designed to do. It is no part of the role of the reserve forces to have forces in being, trained, equipped and ready to fight an equally trained and equipped enemy in instant battle. That is not their job and never has been; and it is a total misconception to consider it as their job.
I must say that the way in which the reserve forces have responded to this appeal reflects the utmost credit on them and on their ability to do a job, and indicates that, just as they did such superb work in raising the nucleus of our forces in the first great war of 1914-18 and in the second world war, they are ready now and will be ready in the future to do the tasks for which they are chosen.
I hope we shall have the strong support not only of the members of the House of Commons but also of the press and of citizens everywhere. This story about keeping the civil servants free from exposure to the dangers of enlistment cannot be calculated to help recruiting or to strengthen the effort to build up Canada's defence forces. I have no doubt that the reporter who obtained the story got it from somebody; but no effort was made to check it with my office, with the chief of the general staff, with the director of public relations, or with the adjutant general; and they are, I think, the only officers qualified to speak authoritatively on a matter of this kind.
The fact that these other reserve army units have not been chosen at this stage does not indicate that they will not have their chance. Our hope is that as this plan develops, each of the reserve force units will make a similar contribution, so that in a

period of two or three years all the reserve force units may have experienced and trained officers and men, who have had recent experience abroad, available to the extent of a company or its equivalent, so that in that way, together with the veterans and the other trained soldiers available, it will greatly shorten the time within which our reserve force will be able to mobilize the force we shall need.
In this plan our intention is to have married men who serve for twelve months overseas and single men who serve for twenty-four months overseas entitled to receive their discharge, although the terms of their military enlistment may not have elapsed. But that of course will depend on the military situation, and we cannot foresee that.
To turn to the question of manpower, while the figures for April are not yet available, estimates show an intake for that month of 2,452 and an outgo of 518, making a net increase of 1,934, which maintains the very good record we have been having, bringing the strength of the three active forces to the figure of 70,361. At this rate, or at anything like it, taken together with the added impetus which we believe will be given by raising the 27th Canadian infantry brigade, it should be possible to see the target for our armed forces and full-time civilian employees of something like 150,000 at March 31, 1954, is likely to be achieved in one-half that time. This target is something which we set down for planning purposes. But we aim to go ahead with our plans and with our programs as fast as the money voted by parliament will permit.
We have had a large number of inquiries from women wishing to join the regular air force or the reserve forces of the three services, in accordance with the announcement I made. As I said then, recruiting for these will not start until the summer, when there will be public announcements. It was not my intention to make this announcement until later. However, a leak occurred, though not through military sources. The article in the R.C.A.F. publication The Roundel, which was said to be the basis for the story referring to W.D.'s in the logistic organization of the armed forces, was actually written more than two years ago, more than two years before the cabinet authorized the recruitment of women. Recruiting will be begun this summer.
We shall have a limited number of places for officers. We mean to have as little overhead as possible, no special establishment and few officers outside of those engaged directly in planning at headquarters, either here or
Supply-National Defence in commands. Women are to be recruited to do particularly work now being done by men, but which can be done as well or better by women, such as radar planning and plotting, radio-teletype communications, clerical duties and the like. Women who believe they have officer qualifications may write to defence headquarters now describing their qualifications either in the services or in civilian life. Their applications will be received and we can process them. Writing in now will not give them a favoured place over those who do not write, or over those whom we may select later.
The white paper and statements made by the Minister of Defence Production deal with
the subject of equipment and I have very little to add at this time. However, I have some new figures which the house has not heard yet, and which may be interesting. In the field of construction, during the period September 30, 1950, to April 30, 1951, there were thirty contracts awarded for construction projects involving amounts of over $500,000 each. During the last six months the Department of Defence Production and Defence Construction Limited have let contracts totalling $520,266,137. During the first six months of the second world war the corresponding figure was $136,120,288.
The appropriation sought for the current fiscal year 1951-52 of $1,600 million, or the amount available for defence purposes from all sources, $1,879 million, may be compared with the expenditures on defence amounting to $195,999,201 in 1947-48; $268,804,813 in 1948-49; $384,879,008 in 1949-50; and $587 million for 1950-51.
At this time last year the appropriation sought was $425 million. The present figure is a little more than four times as much. The appropriation for last year of $425 million was increased by a supplementary vote of $145,200,000 passed at the special session in August, bringing the total up to $567,200,000.

Supply-National Defence To this there should be added a final supplementary adopted in March of $21,575,166, making a total appropriation for 1951 of $588,775,366. Out of this we estimate that we shall spend $587 million, or $1,700,000 less than appropriated.
The table appearing in the white paper at page 29 shows that the figure of $1,879 million is 47'5 per cent of the national budget, 11-67 per cent of the estimated national income for 1951-52, 9-4 per cent of the gross national product for the same year and $134.27 per capita.
This year the official estimates of the federal government amount to $3,586,915,657. Of this a total of no less than $1,365 million are payments fixed by parliament for debt services, subsidies to the provinces, social security payments, or covered by post office revenues and miscellaneous refunds and consequently not subject to government control. The amount of federal government expenditure within the control of the government for all operations of government, apart from defence, is therefore $516,600,000.
In the white paper there are charts showing the distribution of the defence program, measured in dollars and in percentages as between the navy, army and air force, and also between the main objects of expenditure. The percentage of the defence program allotted to the air force shows a steady increase from 25-6 per cent in 1946-47 to 47-8 per cent in the present program. This change in emphasis follows the change in policy adopted by most of our allies; but we by all odds are spending the greatest proportion on air defence of any country in the world. The reasons for that are obvious. We have great facilities for aircraft production and air training. Our record in the air is very definitely a fine one. We have shown that we have the skills not only to fly but to administer, and to train aircrew and groundcrew. We have the skills to keep aircraft flying in the air, and the skills required to make them. And in these respects, with the production of the F-86E, which is moving on well, and production of the CF-100 Canuck, as well as the Orenda engine, and the Beaver, as well as a reconversion program of over 200 aircraft still to be completed, we shall be spending very large sums indeed on the air force for the next three years. During that time we shall acquire or produce a total of no less than 3,300 aircraft.
As I have indicated, this is a three year program. I have seen some criticism on the score that this term is too long, that it should be completed more rapidly. For that matter, one week may be too long. We have no means of telling. But if today we had

all the forces we would like to have at this time we would not be spending $1,879 million on building them up. The same is true of any other country. It is necessary to plan for a period longer than a single year so as to provide for a build-up of personnel, equipment and accommodation that is steady, in balance, co-ordinated and consequently as efficient as possible. This period of three years is being used by a number of the North Atlantic treaty nations. It is the period used in the program of the United Kingdom.
But that is the target. As I have said, we will press on just as fast as we can to do the job, given the resources made available by parliament. As I have said also, it may be estimated that with anything like the current rate of recruitment we will reach the objective as at present planned of having something over 150,000 service personnel and civilians in the armed forces in a year and a half rather than in three years.
May I summarize once again what this program is intended, and what I believe it will enable us, to do. First, to provide for the defence of Canada against direct attack and the protection of our coast and shipping lanes. Second, maintain and reinforce the 25th Canadian infantry brigade in Korea, as well as naval vessels and air force, as long as they are needed in that theatre. Third, build up a brigade group and eleven squadrons for the integrated force in Europe. Fourth, provide for replacements and rotation. Fifth, provide suitable equipment, ships, tanks, aircraft of the latest types for our forces.
It provides also for the build-up of mobilization stores and equipment and a considerable part of the accommodation that might be needed by the forces we would expect to employ in the first year of general war, should there be one. I am sure that that program has the support of every hon. member of the house.
It is possible for us to carry out this substantial program and still balance the budget by reason of the buoyant condition of our economy today. This was made clear by the very comprehensive budget report on the situation presented in this house by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). I assure you, Mr. Chairman, and the committee that we and the armed forces appreciate what it has meant to my colleagues and their departments to make substantial cuts in what in normal times would be a reasonable level of activity for them, in order to make possible a greater national defence effort without upsetting the economy.
This places an even further responsibility on the minister and the Department of

National Defence to observe the utmost in economy. Despite further substantial increases in the size of the armed forces, we plan to have very little increase in the administrative personnel. While we will maintain every effort to effect every possible economy, I should like to say in fairness to our armed forces that our overhead is, I believe, proportionately less than in other comparable countries.
A quantitative test of the extent to which the navy is operational is the proportion of men at sea. In Canada that proportion is about 40 per cent, which is even higher than it was during the war. Members will observe from an answer tabled in the house last Monday that the 15 ships of the Canadian navy in commission during the year 1950 spent a total of 1,724 days at sea as compared with 1,287 days at sea for the 13 ships in 1949 and 1,186 days at sea for the 10 ships in 1948.
Today we have in numbers, although not in formations of men trained and ready to fit into their places in a division, the equivalent of more than a division. If that is taken as the way in which to count the divisional slice, and I suggest that any counting of a divisional slice is a very arbitrary operation and one would have to probe very carefully into any figures given, such as those by the Alsop brothers or any other writers, to make sure of the basis on which they are given, we have a divisional slice which is about half of what we had during the war and considerably less than the reported divisional slice for either the United Kingdom or the United States.
For air forces the test is the number of hours flown per aircraft per month, and in this respect the performance of the R.C.A.F. compares favourably with that of other countries.
This does not mean that we will rest where we are, that this money will be wasted. All the measures of economy that the government, the Department of Finance, the treasury board, the Department of National Defence and the services can bring to bear will be brought to bear and we will see to it that the best possible use is made of this money.
In order that we may have the discussion of these estimates in the order most convenient to members, I would suggest that we follow the practice of recent years. This is entirely a matter for the committee and there is no thought of binding it, but it would be a desirable thing and I am sure one that would meet the views of all quarters of the house if hon. members wishing to make
Supply-National Defence statements about defence generally should do so at the outset. We could then follow with a detailed consideration of the estimates beginning at page 269, taking the main heads in the following order:	administration,
inspection services, civil defence-I would point out that, since the responsibility for civil defence was transferred to the Minister of National Health and Welfare by an order in council dated February 23, this branch of activity falls under that minister and I expect he will be here to make a short statement and to answer any questions-imperial war graves commission, navy, army, air force, defence research, mutual aid, grants, et cetera, pensions.
I repeat that the aim of all this is not war, but peace, peace through the prevention of aggression. With the great efforts being put forth in other countries as well as in Canada, it is our hope, yes, our belief, that we will be able to achieve our objective and preserve peace. With our freedom in the balance, this great effort must be taken and must succeed.

Mr. Chairman, the method of examining these estimates suggested by the minister will, I feel sure, be acceptable to members on this side of the house. Before passing on to the detailed examination of the estimates, I should like to make a few general remarks on the question of defence. In doing so I cannot help but recall the fact that today is the 8th day of May, and the 8th day of May is generally known as V-E day. It is a strange coincidence that on the anniversary of the day when in northwest Europe the cease fire was sounded there will again be Canadian troops landing on foreign soil with many of their former allies in pursuit of those same high ideals.
It has been my privilege, and perhaps my misfortune, to follow the minister immediately after he has completed his statement on the presentation of his annual estimates for the past five or six years. Over this period of time the world situation has demanded a progressively greater proportion of our national budget to be allocated to national defence. Conscious of the deteriorating international situation, the official opposition has never placed any obstacle in the way of the government in raising the funds which the minister has considered necessary to provide this country with reasonable measures of defence. On the contrary, the opposition has frequently taken a lead in urging more effective defence measures and asking for more adequate forces than were being provided in the minister's forecasts in previous years.

Supply-National Defence
We have felt all too frequently in the past that the government has failed to take a realistic view of the state of our armed forces, and that it also failed to relate the state of those forces in true perspective to the dangers which were facing this and other free nations. I am inclined to think that if more heed had been paid to our warnings the development of our forces would have been further advanced today than it is. I am perfectly conscious that I shall be told that the development of such inventions as modern radar, the F-86E and the CF-100 could not have proceeded any faster than it has. I admit quite freely that two years ago I criticized the then F-86, but the F-86 of two years ago and the F-86E of today are quite different aircraft. The F-86E of today has far more thrust and ability to climb, and greater manoeuvrability than the original F-86 ever had.
Perhaps if we had gone ahead and developed the F-86 two years ago we should not have had the same efficient machine that is now being developed, but there are many other fields of activity in which it would have been safe to have gone ahead. We could have increased the number of men and generally raised the state of our armed forces to a much higher degree of efficiency than they have at the present time if the government had listened more to the warnings of the opposition. If that had been done, as the minister has said this afternoon, it would not have been necessary to allocate such a large sum of money for defence as is to be spent this year, the sum of $1,879 million.
Parliament is asked to provide that sum of money to be expended during the present year. If that amount of money had been spread more evenly over the past three years, shall we say, the inflationary tendencies which are so evident today would have been curbed, and also much of the material which we are now purchasing in competition with a booming civilian market could have been purchased at cheaper prices. Thus by delaying war preparedness until this time the government has tended to increase inflation and thereby has placed an additional burden on the taxpayers by increasing the cost of living. I feel that essential materials could have been purchased two, three or four years ago at much reduced prices to those now being paid.
However, I do not intend to engage in what might be called the not unattractive pastime of "I told you so". The recorded debates of this house bear ample evidence of my claim that the opposition has applied the spur to the minister more frequently than the curb.

It has never been an easy task to follow the minister's carefully prepared statement. We have no indication of what is going to be disclosed before the minister makes his statement. The opposition's difficulties are aggravated by a lack of information, and any suggestions which have been advanced to try to make the task of constructive criticism easier for the opposition have been frowned upon by the minister as is the case whenever it has been suggested that a defence committee would assist in that manner.
Today we are perhaps in a little better position than we have been in previous years because the government's program for defence preparedness was announced early in February. Later statements have amplified the general program, and even the white paper issued last night is in the main an amplification of the previous announcements. The minister's speech today, towards the end, most certainly gave us additional information. A good deal of time, not unnaturally, was spent on a historical review of what has been happening in Korea, although at one period in his remarks I thought that we had perhaps wandered into the public accounts committee as he went into considerable detail of how the money had been spent over the last two or three years.
However, he did not follow up that discussion to its logical conclusion by telling us how much of the appropriations is to be allotted for tanks and other equipment out of this year's program. He contented himself by telling us how much had been spent on those particular articles in years gone by. I hope that when we get into the detailed discussion of the various items the minister will then be able to enlighten us and will give us a break-down in corresponding detail, if that is possible.
Recognizing these limitations upon the opposition, Mr. Chairman, we shall do our best to offer some comments on the government's defence program and the manner in which it is proposed to allot the moneys parliament is now being asked to provide in order to implement that program. Before reviewing the program itself, however, I should like to join with the minister and pay my tribute and the tribute of the opposition members to the gallant men of the Royal Canadian Navy now serving in far eastern waters with the various Canadian destroyers; to the men of the 25th brigade now in Korea; and to the men of 426 transport squadron of the R.C.A.F. It goes without saying that in the past months these men have lived up to the highest traditions of Canadians who in previous wars have fought for the freedom of

this land, and that they will continue to do so in future.
As in previous wars, all parts of Canada are represented. I was pleased to hear the minister refer to the contribution being made by the province of Quebec and our Frenchspeaking Canadians. When I went to Fort Lewis in January I was impressed by the efficiency of the Royal 22nd Regiment, both the second and third battalions, and by French-speaking soldiers serving with other units, who did not come solely from the province of Quebec. I endorse what the minister has said, and add that I believe all sections of this country have responded to the call equally in proportion to the population of the various racial divisions of our country. While at Fort Lewis I was impressed by the similarity of outlook in all units, and by the spirit of true comradeship which existed not only within the units themselves but between the various units of the brigade. There was a common desire to do the job at hand, with little or no unhealthy rivalry as between the various units. Nor would I like this occasion to pass without making reference to the sacrifices being made by our allies whose forces are fighting in Korea under the flag of the United Nations. It was with particular interest that we read a few days ago of the magnificent stand made by the Gloucestershire Regiment. I single out that regiment because for many years the Gloucestershire has been allied with the senior infantry regiment in the Canadian army, the Royal Canadian Regiment. It is of interest to note that once again the Gloucestershire Regiment and the Royal Canadian Regiment will be fighting side by side.
The estimates we are now to consider are designed to implement the program first announced by the minister on February 5 and repeated on several occasions since. The international background which has necessitated these expanded defence measures was explained in the house yesterday. It is a confused and complex situation, which has forced many nations to abandon their traditional foreign policies. There is an indication that for many years we shall have to live in an atmosphere of high tension. There can be no peace with the rulers in the Kremlin, because there is no basis of understanding with men whose superiority complex and sense of omnipotence would mould all the peoples of this planet into their way of thinking. Yet there must be no war, in spite of an understandable desire to cut short this period of tension. Thus we have the paradoxical situation of no peace and no war. To that end the free nations must be strong enough to thwart communist designs for world-wide
Supply-National Defence aggression, and at the same time must exercise sufficient restraint to make the enemy realize that we will not easily be provoked into open warfare.
The blueprint of the government's program to meet this ambiguous situation was announced on February 5, when it received the general support of the opposition. In very brief outline the blueprint, if I may call it such, indicates that there will be 100 ships in the Royal Canadian Navy, with many small craft, either new or refitted or newly armed. As far as the army is concerned there will be the airborne striking force, anti-aircraft artillery and other units for the defence of Canada against direct attack. There will be the part of the army with General Eisenhower's force. The extent of that contribution was announced just a couple of days ago; we are to raise, train and equip the 27th brigade. Part of the Canadian force will still be serving in the Far East, and steps are to be taken to rotate the personnel who are there. In addition we are to maintain administrative staff, training establishments, depots, stores, clothing and equipment to provide for rapid mobilization should a total war effort be required. When we turn to the Royal Canadian Air Force, we are to have forty regular and reserve squadrons with more than 3,000 aircraft in addition to those we now have. There is to be an extension of the radar system, which is to be fully manned. In Europe we are to have an air division of some eleven fighter squadrons, and airfields, men and equipment to train large numbers of aircrew for ourselves and other countries.
That, in brief, is the blueprint of the program. We are told that in order to carry out these commitments the strength of the service is to be increased to about 115,000 fulltime, active service personnel, and the minister repeated that figure today. That, I fear, is an understatement of the manpower requirement. I feel it is a miscalculation which may throw out of gear the whole concept of our plan. I do not believe 115,000 men will be sufficient to meet all those commitments which were announced on February 5 and repeated today.
