The figure previously
announced was 115,000, and I do not feel that this would meet all the commitments that have been indicated. The minister has stressed the accelerated recruitment. In previous discussions during this session I said, and I meant it, that we should endeavour to assist the minister to obtain the men that are required. I believe that many members on

Supply-National Defence all sides of the house have already lent their aid and influence in the recruiting of the personnel required.
During the first three months of this year there has been a steady increase, though I do not think it is a spectacular increase. For the navy, at the end of 1950, there were 10,184, all ranks; by the end of March, according to the figures published in this white paper, there were 11,082. The increase from the end of the year for the army was from 32,456 to 34,986; for the R.C.A.F., from 18,436 to 22,359. From the figures which were given by the minister a few minutes ago it would seem that the same rate of increase was maintained during the month of April, roughly speaking about 2,000 for all three services every month. We must face up to the fact that the early months of any year is the period of time when there is more unemployment in the land. I believe one would be optimistic to believe that for the next three months we shall be able to maintain that same rate of increase. I hope we can, but it may require renewed and more vigorous efforts on the part of the government.
There is a point regarding this recruitment which I believe should be brought to the committee's attention. These men have been recruited, may I say, in the haphazard manner in which Canada has always mobilized her manpower for war. Little, if any, consideration has been given to the needs of industry, agriculture or war industry. Lessons that might have been learned, I fear, have not been heeded. Even when this government at the beginning of this session, prompted by outside sources, set up a manpower advisory council, we find that that council has been submerged in a morass of procrastination. The council was authorized on February 1, and since that date has held but one meeting. Thus we drift along in the same old way, leaving it entirely to chance whether a recruit volunteers for service in the particular section of the armed forces for which he is best suited, if indeed he is better suited for the armed force's than for defence production, industry or agriculture. The decision is left entirely to the recruit who, having very little knowledge of the requirements, must decide between the appeals of the minister for defence and the minister for defence production. The delay in calling a second meeting of this manpower advisory council is, in my opinion, unforgivable.
I hope that the same haste will not be displayed in the recruiting of the 27th brigade that was seen during the period of the recruitment of the Korean force. I am rather suspicious of the figures which were

announced by the minister today, 1,200 applications having been received during the first day of recruiting for the 27th brigade. The result of that hasty recruiting for the Korean force was that over 700 men were discharged as being medically unfit, and others were discharged within a few months for other reasons. There is not the same haste today to recruit the 27th brigade as there was to recruit the 25th brigade. Whether or not there is a need for speed, I do stress the importance of a thorough medical examination before anyone is enlisted into the force. Time will be saved in the long run, and a great deal of expense will be saved the Canadian taxpayers.
The minister stated that the recruiting drive to mobilize the 27th brigade commenced yesterday. The difficulties and petty annoyances that arose in connection with the organization of the 25th brigade or the special Korean force will, I hope, be avoided. On the fourth of May the minister stated that there is only one Canadian army today, and that is a most desirable condition. I hope that ideal will be maintained. We came very close to having a two-army system last fall as a result of the manner in which the special force was raised. Figures have been given concerning the supply of officers for the services. While it may be comforting to know -these figures were given in the white paper -that there is available a pool of some 57,000 veteran officers from world war II, we must not overlook the fact that advancing years will disqualify, if they have not already done so, many of these veteran officers. Young leaders are required. I was rather surprised at the very small quotas which had been allotted to the officers' training establishment in the various universities. According to figures which were given to me in reply to a question I asked a few days ago to all intents and purposes the universities across the country reached the quotas which were allocated to them. This is an indication that the universities and the university students are prepared to do, and are doing, their full share in this respect.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The quotas were virtually adjusted to what the universities could do. We hope they are going to do more.
As I say, practically every university fulfilled the quota which had been given to it. I believe that is very commendable, but I am going to ask you to increase those quotas in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We shall ask them to do everything they can.

There is no obligation upon these university students who go through officer training classes to join one or the other of the services. At the same time, that is a method which has created an available pool of young leaders, and I have sufficient confidence in young Canada to believe a large proportion of them will respond to the call.
In view of the expansion contemplated for the forces, and the officer requirement, I am wondering whether we are getting full value from the two service colleges. I am inclined to think that the four-year course, without the obligation of joining the active forces at the conclusion of those four years, may be a luxury which we can hardly afforded to maintain in the present crisis. It may therefore be necessary at this time to introduce some modification of the terms for admittance to those colleges and the length of the various courses; because the output from those colleges at the present time is almost negligible in relation to the demand.
I have just one other observation to make with regard to state-assisted education. It does not always seem to produce the results that are expected. Many veterans of world war II were given college educations at the conclusion of hostilities, in accordance with the rehabilitation plan. I sincerely hope that the other professions have responded more readily than has the medical profession; because I was greatly surprised to find that only two medical officers with the Korean force were medical men who were not in the active army. I do not think that fact reflects high credit on the medical profession as a whole and I cannot help wondering-and I should like the minister to be able to tell me- what percentage of the technical officers trained under our rehabilitation plan after the last war are now serving in the forces at the present time.
I now turn to another point. I cannot help expressing some regret at the indifferent results which have been achieved in the sphere of standardization of arms among the forces of the north Atlantic powers. That Canada should be in the process of exchanging United Kingdom types for United States types can hardly be called standardization. If we have sent to the United Kingdom equipment for three divisions for Europe, it has not yet been replaced by United States types. I would have hoped that we should have reached a stage by now when European countries and American countries could use far more of the same type of arms and equipment than they are apparently using today. Standardization has hardly begun. I hope that the government will use every effort to 80709-179J
Supply-National Defence further the desirable objective of standardization which is required. There is still uncertainty even as to the type of rifle that the troops are to carry. When that decision is made as to what rifle we in Canada are to have, I hope that we shall at least see the three services carrying the same rifle.
The same uncertainty exists in regard to the light machine gun. Is it still to be the Bren gun? If so, it should be remodelled to conform either with the British .280 or with the United States .300. If we are to keep it, a decision must be reached to remodel the Bren gun along one of those lines; or, if we are going to discard it altogether, then the sooner we know what is to replace it, the better. You cannot go into action with a small unit having many different calibres of ammunition.
Another point on the same matter of arms is this. We note that some 400 3-7" ack-ack guns have been sent to Europe. These are to be replaced by United States 90 millimetre guns.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Excuse me, they have not been sent; they will be sent if arrangements can be made.

Oh, they will be sent? The wording I have here is that they have been sent, but apparently that is an error. I hope that no time will be lost between the date when these 3 [DOT] 7's go and the date when the 90 millimetre guns replace them.
To come to the question of armament within the services, in previous years the minister has made much of the unification among the three services. We find that this policy in some respects does not appear to be continuing; in fact, it appears to be discontinued at least in so far as the operation, maintenance and repair of motor transport is concerned because each of the armed services-the navy, the army and the air force-has now reverted to its own methods of maintenance and has assumed the responsibility for the repair of its own. vehicles.
Surely the maintenance of motor vehicles of a similar type should have been coordinated and should remain co-ordinated and uniform if the principle of unification is to hold. Has that principle of unification failed? Or is the desire to work together lacking amongst some of the forces? A coordinated or unified policy, though the various services may at times have to go through a slimming process, is far more likely to produce economical and effective results than is a system under which each of the services is working on its own. I cannot help feeling that the reversal of this policy with respect

Supply-National Defence to the care, maintenance, operation and repair of motor vehicles is detrimental. I have never known an admiral, a general or an air marshal who did not begin by asking for more than his share of anyining. With social security expenditures as they are today, it becomes all the more necessary that the department should place orders only for militr ry stores which are absolutely essential.
I have a few remarks I wish to make with regard to the navy. The role of the navy has, I think, been described in this way: The primary responsibility of the Royal Canadian Navy is that of anti-submarine activities. It is interesting to note that with the outbreak of world war I German submarine attacks struck a serious blow at the Royal Navy by sinking three British cruisers in home waters. This success was followed, both in world war I and in world war II, by submarine attacks on warships, merchant vessels and upon the life line of the nations then at war. Between 1914 and 1918, 4,837 merchant ships were sunk. In world war II 2,775 merchant ships were sunk. During those two wars the submarine came nearer than any other weapon to causing our defeat. Since the cessation of hostilities in world war II great developments have taken place, so far as submarine warfare is concerned. According to the semi-official publication, Jane's Fighting Ships, the Russians have .some 750 modern submarines at the present time. Anti-submarine defence demands closely [DOT]co-ordinated teams to search out and to [DOT]destroy hostile submerged craft. Obviously the inclusion of aircraft in these anti-submarine teams is indicated. It may be assumed That landbased aircraft would be useful within certain specific distances, provided suitable airfields are available on each coast. But for mid-ocean operations it is still I believe the opinion of naval authorities that the air component of these teams can best oe supplied by a carrier.
The experience of the last war indicated that carrier-borne aircraft could keep submarine sinkings down. Fighter aircraft, as well as reconnaissance aircraft, must be included in our anti-submarine teams. For years the minister has been calling attention to the development of our new antisubmarine vessels. I do not know how much longer we are to wait for the commissioning of these vessels. I hope every effort will be made to speed up the construction of these new anti-submarine vessels, so that we may not have to rely solely upon the reconverting of the older types.
Today Canada really has no effective antisubmarine teams. During the past year Magnificent, accompanied by destroyers, *carried out training cruises in anti-submarine
[Mr. Pearkes.i
warfare. If those tests proved anything, they showed the ineffectiveness and vulnerability of the combination. Magnificent is out of date, and the 16 Sea Furies and 20 Firefly aircraft of the skeleton air groups are totally inadequate for the protection of our two oceans.
Nor can Magnificent take on her landing decks modern aircraft of the jet-propelled type used in submarine searches. It will be necessary in a very short time either to remodel Magnificent or to exchange her for another more up-to-date vessel.
I repeat the statement I made a year ago, that if it is considered desirable for an aircraft carrier to be maintained on the Atlantic, with some four naval aviation squadrons, then some protection of a similar nature should be provided for the Pacific, where the ocean spaces are wider and the facilities for land-based aircraft are less, because the coastal airfields on the Pacific coast have not been maintained adequately since the war.
Reference was made a year ago to the division of the Royal Canadian Navy into operational and training groups. To what extent has that policy been developed? I understand that our second cruiser is being recommissioned. When I first suggested this to the minister he advised me that this was not desirable because the cruiser strength of the United Nations was considered more than adequate. What is the reason for this change in policy in less than twelve months? Is the cruiser Uganda, now renamed Quebec, to be used purely as a training ship, like Ontario? I presume that is the reason.
That brings me to the point as to whether or not these cruisers are really the best type of ship to provide the opportunities we require for the training of navy personnel to meet the role envisaged for the Royal Canadian Navy, namely that of anti-submarine warfare. Cruisers are expensive ships to maintain. Official figures indicate that it cost over $10,000 a day to operate and maintain Ontario at sea. Of course it costs nothing like that amount to operate and maintain a destroyer. Consideration should be given to the point of whether we can afford to maintain ships of the Ontario type purely for training purposes when, as I say, it costs over $10,000 a day while they are at sea.
The minister indicated that nearly one hundred ships and many small craft, either new or refitted, will be commissioned during the next three years. This will provide a very considerable force, but I suggest that far more information is required on the subject,

which I hope the minister will be able to give when we are dealing with details. Numbers may be grossly misleading. It is obviously a waste of money, though, to keep obsolete ships in reserve. Of course it would be a waste of the lives of young Canadians to man old outworn ships for another shooting war; but we cannot or should not keep in reserve obsolete ships in our yards.
In reply to an official request I was informed that it costs $133 a day to keep a destroyer in reserve, and $83 to keep a frigate. One can see that these figures quickly mount up. If we are to obtain no value from keeping these ships in reserve, then I suggest it would be much better to send them to the scrap pile and have them broken up for steel.
I should1 like to say this regarding the army. Now is the time to consider providing winter quarters for such troops as will be in training next winter. We cannot afford the luxury of sending troops out of the country, with additional pay, because we do not have winter training quarters. I would ask the minister, when he replies, to tell us how much it is costing the country in additional pay to send the troops to Fort Lewis. I do not know whether the United States asked rental for their buildings, but I suggest we should have information on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I should be glad to give it. They made a very fair arrangement.

I have only one or two remarks to make concerning the Royal Canadian Air Force. I should like to sound a warning about the multiplicity of types. I hope we will concentrate on those essential types which will fit in with our particular role. I was not impressed with the marine reconnaissance aircraft being converted from the Lancaster that I saw recently. I question very much whether that would be a suitable type.
I know it will take another year before the full results can be seen from the construction of our new aircraft. We should not delay in getting crews ready so that as soon as these plants go into full production the crews will be ready and available to man the aircraft.
I hope that the minister will give the minister who is responsible for civilian defence an opportunity to make a statement before we go into a detailed consideration of the various items. There might be some general remarks we should like to have. As far as this government considers it necessary to raise troops for the defence of Canada, to repress
Supply-National Defence aggression and for the maintenance of those ideals and principles which all three nations have, they will never find the opposition putting obstacles in the way of any well thought out plan.

Mr. Chairman, this discussion today on defence estimates follows logically the discussion we had yesterday on external affairs. After all, the necessity for defence arises out of the international situation. I think if the people of Canada understand the international situation they will be glad indeed to do what the hon. member for Nanaimo has just suggested, act in unity to prevent aggression against this country and the overthrow of the institutions of democracy which mankind possesses.
In his introductory remarks this afternoon the minister recognized that defence involves more than military preparedness. As I would have expected him to do, he remarked that if we are going to maintain unity in our country and across the world for the defence of democratic institutions we must embark, on plans to raise the standards of living and to safeguard and even extend the freedoms that we have. With that sentiment I agree thoroughly.
I want also to join with the hon. member for Nanaimo and the minister in paying a brief tribute to our armed forces fighting in Korea, the army in the field, the navy in the adjacent waters and the R.C.A.F. squadron which is participating in that remarkable airlift from North America to Japan. I think Canada can be proud of those men. In expressing pride in their achievements one also would like to express deep sympathy with those who mourn the loss of the young men who have fallen already in Korea.
It was indeed satisfactory that the minister was able to place before the committee evidence that the appeal by the armed forces has met with response from all parts of Canada, that no part has fallen down inproviding its quota of young men for the forces of Canada. I remember the occasion in late September 1944 when I, along with the hon. member for Melfort and the hon. member for Cape Breton South, made up the first civilian party from Canada to visit the cemetery at Dieppe. At that time not all the crosses had been erected, but I remember so well walking down the rows of crosses and noting the names, largely those of the men in whom I was interested, those of the South Saskatchewan Regiment. I noted that these names indicated various religious and racial backgrounds, French, Ukrainian, Jewish, Scandinavian, English, Polish, even German and so on. There they were lying

Supply-National Defence together in the cemetery representing the diverse peoples who are helping to build this Canada of ours.
I am going to ask the minister if anything is being done similar to that which was done in the last war to inform the young men who are fighting in the Korean war as to what they are fighting for. I remember I asked this question last September. It was prompted by the fact that on a previous Sunday evening I had heard a broadcast of a discussion between a Toronto newspaperman and United States reporters in Tokyo. The newspaperman was J. B. McGeachy and he was asking what had been done to inform the young men who were fighting as to what they were fighting for. I remember that the United States correspondents in Tokyo could not answer that question; indeed they did not seem to understand what the question involved.
About a week or ten days ago I was visited by a Canadian lady and gentleman who have a son, a lieutenant, in the United States air forces. That son is back in the United States having suffered injuries in Korea. They had visited him and his comrades, in hospital. They told me that that lad and the young men with him were puzzled as to why they had been in Korea and for what they were fighting in that country. When hon. members get the Ottawa Citizen a little later this evening, if they will turn to the editorial page they will find some questions asked by a Canadian journalist and answers by another Canadian journalist, who is also apparently an editor of Maclean's magazine and recently returned from Korea. The first question was whether our boys overseas Know what they are fighting for and what it is all about. The answer given is that most of the officers know, but almost invariably the men cannot answer the question as to why they are there and what they are fighting for.
Since we were so successful in the last war in informing the young men in the armed forces of Canada and in the allied forces as to what the war was all about, I think steps should be taken again to inform the young men engaged in the struggle in Korea as to why they are there and what they are fighting for. I believe that they are there because an act of aggression was committed by North Korean forces last June. They are fighting to prevent further communist aggression in other places in the future. That is one point the department might keep in mind.
Last autumn and again yesterday I said that in building up our defence forces I think the first step should be, and it may still be

advisable to do it, to make a thorough appraisal of our resources. I noted that the hon. member for Nanaimo in the excellent speech he made a few minutes ago spoke of present recruiting and the necessity of considering the interests of industry and agriculture, both vital to our defence effort. It seems to me that in order to do that efficiently we need to have an appraisal of our manpower resources to a greater extent than is being made by the manpower committee. Further, that appraisal should also involve an appraisal of the industrial possibilities of Canada, of agriculture and of our natural resources because should war come I think that Canada's principal contribution may still be not in the realm, of armed forces but rather, remote as we hope to be although we may not be altogether as remote as the last time from the threat of bombing, that we may be called upon to contribute very heavily to the equipment of such armed forces as there may be and for the production of vast quantities of food and raw materials. Therefore we need to adopt a policy of defence which involves more than merely the provision of armed forces, although that must be a vital part of any defence effort that we make.
In that connection we have to consider the relationship of several fields of defence in which we may be called upon to operate. First there is Canada's own defence, including of course civilian defence against the effects of spasmodic bombing. Then there is our continental defence, our contribution to the defence of the northern part of North America, because perchance this time there may be sporadic raids across the pole, across Siberia, over Alaska, and attempts made indeed to land raiding parties from the air to dislocate our industrial life through the northern reaches of our country. Third, we have of course the obligations we have assumed under the North Atlantic alliance. Lastly, there are our obligations under the United Nations. The obligations that we have thus assumed are very great, very wide. They will demand a great expenditure of effort and of money on the part of Canada.
One of the first things that could have been done, I think, in placing the problem of defence before the house was for the minister, and indeed other members of the government, to have made very comprehensive statements regarding our obligations, and what we are expected to do in the respective fields in which we have made most substantial commitments. You know, from listening to the ministers, and from reading the transcripts of the discussions in the public accounts committee, I think the position of

Canada seems to be that which was stated in yesterday's issue of Time magazine with relation to Washington. Hon. members who have read it will probably remember that the article contained the following:
What could a nation make of a leadership whose top military men discoursed confidently of their forces, not the forces of today, but what they plan to have two years from now?
It seems to me that one of the weaknesses in our discussions of defence is that we are talking about the equipment, men and so on that we expect to have two years from now, and we are not paying sufficient attention as a parliament to what we already have. I say to the minister that I think some opportunity should be given hon. members to understand more precisely what the government is doing. I think there would be much more confidence in the department if hon. members were better informed as to what the department is actually doing. I remember that during the last war we had a war expenditures committee. That committee met in camera quite often. Officials of the department came before the committee, and we were often given quite vital and confidential information regarding equipment, supplies, and new methods of war.
I remember very distinctly that some quite secret and confidential explosives were shown to us long before they were used. Their use was explained and the reason why we had appropriated sums of money in order that the experiments leading up to the production of the explosives might be made. In parliament we have no means of knowing exactly what the government is doing ini many respects. Obviously, there are some questions that hon. members are reluctant to ask on the floor of the house or in a committee of this description, but they are questions which should be answered. As I said, I think that a committee like the war expenditures committee, before which departmental officials could appear, and to which information could be given which in the interests of security could not be given in committee of supply or in a public session of the house, should be set up in order that those members of the house who would be members of the committee would be able to reassure their colleagues in the same confidential manner.
In the second world war I do not remember a single instance during the existence of the war expenditures committee when anything of a secret or confidential nature was divulged improperly. I think it would be well if something of that sort could be done again in the interests of unity in the house, and in order to give the house confidence in

Someone has said that the public accounts committee can make inquiries, but the public accounts committee is limited to the fiscal year ending on the 31st of March, 1950, the last public accounts available.

precisely. We want to know what has transpired during the fourteen months that have elapsed. When the house adopted Bill No. 133 last year we surrendered a good many of our rights to the government and to the Department of National Defence. The measure gave the cabinet power to decide the number and extent of the armed forces, for example, something which prior to that time always had to be approved by parliament. We gave the minister great powers under that measure. I think the house agreed to the bill rather reluctantly because we believed that there was tremendous urgency to get certain things done, and we were very uncertain as to what was going to happen in the immediate future. But what progress has been made during the past year in obtaining the equipment for which large sums have been appropriated? This afternoon the minister mentioned many millions of dollars of equipment authorized through defence production, but how much of that equipment has been obtained? To what extent has defence production placed orders for that equipment with the industrial groups which can provide it? In February the hon. member for Moose Jaw asked some questions and on February 23 this year a return was brought down. The questions were these:

The answers were:

Then there was this further question:

The answer was:

The next question was:
Has any of the equipment been actually turned over to the defence forces?
The answer was yes; but as of that date in February, defence contracts for transportation equipment and so on had been let to the extent of only two and a half million dollars, and apparently the situation is not very much better now. I have a Canadian

Supply-National Defence Press dispatch dated Windsor, April 30, 1951, containing a report of the annual statement of the president of the Ford Motor Company to his shareholders, and I think perhaps I had better read it in case the minister should want to comment on it:
In his annual report to shareholders here today, Rhys M. Sale, president of Ford of Canada, said he wanted to "clear the air" of misleading and conflicting stories about the defence production role of his company by saying that "up to this moment" Ford has not been called upon to participate in the national preparedness program.
After reporting that 800 workers had been laid off because necessary steel parts were not available from the United States, Mr. Sale said it would be wasteful for any part of the Ford plant or any number of its workers to stand idle when Canada needs to strengthen its defensive power.
Mr. Sale announced that a major expansion in manufacturing facilities will get under way at the giant Windsor plant "as soon as circumstances permit." He added the company is not yet ready to announce the nature of the project.
The Ford president said, however, that work on a large central parts depot here, as well as similar depots at Montreal1 and Regina has been held1 up indefinitely because the company has been unable to obtain construction permits from Ottawa Mr. Sale said "almost daily increases in material costs and a further demand for substantial wage increases" may leave the company with no alternative but to raise prices on its products.
Mr. Sale said the company has had an inquiry from the government about producing a special military jeep. If the company got the contract, he remarked, it would not "provide an answer, in any sense, to the possible unemployment problem that may result from material shortages or reduced sales."
To me that statement is very disturbing, first because it indicates a failure to grant the necessary permits-though this does not concern the minister-for the expansion of the industry when- material becomes available; and that in the face of the needs the minister outlined this afternoon. It is disturbing in the second place because it indicates a lack of co-operation between the United States and Canada in the matter of certain parts and supplies; and the third reason it is disturbing, of course, is because of the prospect of unemployment in the industry. It further indicates, of course, that rising prices may once again reduce the value of our defence dollar.
These are matters of the type into which more careful inquiry should be made than is possible in this committee, or during a formal house debate. A special committee of parliament, similar to the committee on war expenditures which we had during the last war and which functioned so well, I think would be useful and would be warranted. Then we are told there is some difficulty due to the hesitation of the United States in placing substantial orders in Canada in order that we may get the necessary United
[Mr. Coldwell.l

I noticed that early last month the Minister of National Defence made a speech in New York in which he said the Canadian government had placed $159 million in firm orders in the United States for various defence materials, as against only $9 million of firm United States orders placed in Canada; and I believe he also said we expected to place something like $300 million of orders in the United States in the current financial year. Is our production being retarded through lack of co-operation by the United States in the provision of vital parts? If so, I think publicity should be given the matter, and every effort should be made to remedy the situation. I have no doubt that has been done already.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly, though I may not be able to answer it.

-as to what the government is doing or what the policy is. As a member of this house I am not well informed on such matters because we do not get the information that we require. There is no facility for getting it at the present time. Let us have a committee like the war expenditures committee in which we can get the information, and get matters straightened out.
Another question I am going to ask is this. To what extent do customs duties and red tape interfere with the exchange of supplies and commodities amongst the north Atlantic nations? I understand that there is free entry, on a reciprocal basis, of war equipment and the personal belongings of people who are engaged in active service, but that that does not apply to component parts which are purchased by firms engaged on defence contracts. What is the state of our equipment? I am talking about the information that was given in the public accounts committee this morning. I have no doubt that the minister will have a very good reply to what I am saying. What I am complaining about is that this parliament does not know. I am not attacking the minister or his department. The member for Nanaimo mentioned jeeps. I want to ask the minister if the manufacture of jeeps in this country has been held up because of difficulties with patents. Is that so? If it is so, then efforts should be made to overcome that difficulty. Immediately I say that, I know the difficulty of getting the tools and all the rest of it for new types of planes. But that was in the year 1950. For 1951 we have been told the expenditure was greater than $30 million, how much greater I do not know because we have not the record before us. Is it correct that only two CF-100 planes were produced during that year, one of which was subsequently lost? This afternoon the minister said we would be getting some F-86's. Have we any yet? Have any been turned out on the assembly line? We do not know. The government is responsible to this house, but we members of the house are responsible to our constituents. We are responsible to the people who expect this department to defend them. We are responsible to the people whose taxes will provide the money to purchase that equipment, and there is not one of us who can answer the two questions that I have just asked. The minister may answer them or he may not answer them. It may not be advisable to answer them. Again, that is an answer that could be given to a confidential committee or a committee sitting in camera.
Of course, these questions are asked in the public accounts committee, a public meeting.
I can understand the reluctance to answer these questions, and I am not pressing that such questions should be answered.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Both those questions have already been answered.
Have they been answered?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The information is quite widely known publicly.

Then I have not seen it in the record or in the press, so I must have missed something.
The hon. member for Nanaimo touched on che question of co-ordinating the forces of Canada. According to the records of the last war the lack of co-ordination created some difficulties. I suppose in order to bring about


some co-ordination the government recently appointed a chairman of the staff committee, Lieutenant General Foulkes. I do not know what his authority is or what his powers are. Does it mean that, in effect, we now have a supreme commander of our Canadian forces, and that this has not only been done to co-ordinate the forces of Canada but to eliminate the kind of rivalry one is bound to find when you have three organizations under three separate heads more or less independent except that they are answerable to the minister? I believe some mention should be made of the fact that there is considerable duplication of effort in these three services. As far as I know only one service of great importance to the three forces is unified; I refer to the dental service. We have three medical corps, three nursing services- and three hospital services. It seems to me, as it has always seemed, that there is no reason in the world why we could not have one medical, nursing and hospital service in the armed forces of Canada and thus prevent the duplication, and apparent waste of medical personnel that has occurred. I know of course that where you have a hospital in an area under control of one of the forces, members of the other armed forces are admitted to it. But in the interests of economy and efficiency in administration, I think that one over-all medical, nursing and hospital plan would eliminate a good deal of waste and a good deal of duplication in the armed services.
The same thing applies, of course, to many of the supplies. I have even read that there is not a common attestation form for the three forces, and that each force has its own types of stationery, forms and all that kind of thing, when many of them might be common to them all.
Let me say just one other word-I will try to conclude now-and that has to do with the reserve forces. I noted what the minister said some time ago, namely that after all the reserve force must be the foundation of the armed forces of Canada. When we look at the record in the report of the Minister of National Defence for the year ending March 31, 1950, we note this in appendix 3 on page 88. If we look at the reserve force, making a comparison with the years 1937-38 or 1935-36 and coming right down to 1949-50, which is the best year since 1945-46, we find 43,047 in the reserve force in 1949-50. In 1939-40 we had 46,855; in 1938-39 we had 51,418; and in 1937-38 we had 45,631 and so on back to 1925-26 when we had 49,075. In other words, the numbers in the reserve

force at the moment are low in comparison with the number prior to the second world war.
The minister this afternoon perhaps gave a partial explanation of that fact when he said that they had called on the reserve force to provide companies or groups to join some of the famous regiments of Canada. That may in part account for this fact. But at the same time I think that all of us in the House of Commons should endeavour to assist the minister and the department in getting young men in the country to train in the reserve force. I think many hon. members have done so. At the same time I think that the department should consider ways and means of offering to young men more inducements than now exist to join the reserve force. I know a suggestion has been made that any pay they receive in connection with the reserve force should be exempt from income tax. Another suggestion that has been made is that they should be allowed something for transportation when they have to travel to the armouries, that better facilities should be provided for training and so on. I think that anything within reason the department can do to make the reserve force more attractive should be done.
All parties in this chamber want to avoid anything in the nature of compulsion. Therefore, because we believe that we should have recruiting for all our armed forces on a voluntary basis, we should co-operate with the department as closely as we can in order to get the results that are necessary. I think the minister is quite right in stating that in the past the reserve forces have been the basis upon which the active forces, when they were needed, were formed and from which recruits were obtained.
There were several other matters about which I intended to say something, but another opportunity will be provided in the discussion on the estimates. I want to assure the minister that the points I have raised this afternoon have been raised in order that members of the House of Commons, and myself as a member, may be informed more completely of what the situation is in the realm of national defence and of what the department and the government are doing to see that the moneys we are appropriating are well spent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the committee understands my feelings, that if parliament insists that we are going to deal with these divorce bills here, then we should deal with them in a responsible manner. I do not think we should just pass them en masse without getting certain information, and making sure that we are competent in each case to pass the bill. I would ask the hon. member for Lisgar, who is responsible for the bill, if there are any children in this family?

Perhaps I might be permitted to say at this point-and this will probably answer a number of other questions the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre might ask-that these bills may be sponsored by any member of the House of Commons. In recent years it has been the practice to send bills to the chairman of the committee for signature.
I have done some research work, although possibly not in any amount comparable with that done by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, in an effort to find out the responsibilities of a member sponsoring these bills, and particularly the responsibilities of the chairman of the committee. I found in the fourth edition of Bourinot that divorces were granted as early as 1835, which was long before confederation, and that at the time of confederation parliament was given jurisdiction over divorce. Therefore it has been more or less an accomplished proceeding. Looking at the Votes and Proceedings for May 1, I find, as indicated at page 326, that a long list of divorce bills was presented to the house. These bills have been sent to us from the other house, which recommends that the marriages be dissolved and asks that we give consideration to their adoption. I am sorry I cannot locate the exact words. In view of that, when these bills are sent to my office from the office of the Clerk I sign them without any hesitation. I do not even look at the name on the bill. I take it for granted that the thing has been gone into thoroughly in the other house and that is sufficient for me.
I have satisfied myself that the other house is quite competent in every respect to deal with these things. When they send bills to this house asking for our approval, I am quite satisfied to sign them. I do not think it is my duty to do research work on all these bills and find out particulars such as those asked for by the hon. member in regard to children and dependents. That matter is considered most carefully in every divorce petition.
I do not see why I should be compelled to make statistics which any hon. member can make for himself. He can have his stenographer study the reports which are sent to every member of parliament and make any statistics he wishes. I would be permanently busy making statistics in regard to divorce bills if I were so inclined. Until I have some positive instructions in that regard I do not intend to do anything about it. Consequently I cannot give the hon. member the information he asks for. I have looked into some of these proceedings, but unless I am given other instructions in that

regard I do not intend to make up statistics in regard to the details of these bills.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon.
member for Lisgar knows full well that when I speak on this matter I am not speaking against him personally in any way whatsoever. He and I are good friends. But it does seem to me that what he has said just now makes the practice through which we go in this House of Commons even more ridiculous than it seemed before. The hon. member permits his name to appear on the order paper two or three hundred times a year as the sponsor of these bills and he now tells us that he signs his name to these bills as chairman of the committee on miscellaneous private bills without even looking to see what names are involved in the divorces he sponsors.
He may be signing his name some day to a bill which will break up one of the happy families around this house. I suggest that he should be more careful. The hon. member has suggested that if I want the information I started to ask for I could ask my stenographer to read these reports that come to our desks and compile the information. I have more respect for my stenographer than to ask her to undertake that kind of chore. As a matter of fact I do not think that any of us were sent here by our constituents to do the kind, of research work that is suggested. The hon. member is suggesting that we should go through these cases individually in order to get any information that we may want.
I do not know the parties involved in this first bill. As is her right, Mrs. McRandall has come to parliament to ask for a divorce, and no doubt she is entitled to it. But surely this House of Commons should not be asked to approve of this bill without our being able to get information along the lines I have suggested. It seems to me that we should know whether the McRandalls had any children and, if so, what arrangements have been made for them or what arrangements are contemplated.
My understanding is that an act of parliament dissolving a marriage does not deal with the children at all. I understand that if there are children, proceedings must be taken before an appropriate court. I think we should know the circumstances in that connection before we are asked to approve of this divorce. We should know whether the sponsor of this bill is satisfied that Mrs. McRandall is the innocent party. We should know whether there has been proof that there was no collusion leading up to the petition for divorce. In view of the fact that parliament has decided that we are not

going to transfer this business somewhere else, we as responsible members of parliament should undertake this job in a responsible way and find out whether we are competent to grant the divorce set out in Bill No. 103.

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is making an appropriate and effective protest against this method of dealing with divorce. There are over 100 bills in this list and we are asked to give approval without having; any knowledge of what is involved. It is all very well to say that a committee in the other place does go into each case separately. I am free to confess that after having seen what is done there on one or two occasions the inquiry is not as perfunctory as it appeared to be at one time. But none the less I think it is time that this House of Commons objected to this manner of dealing with the solemn matter of the dissolution of marriage.
I do not think divorce should be encouraged; indeed I believe quite the opposite, but none the less if divorce is requested by an aggrieved person, that divorce should foe granted only after a proper judicial inquiry. I know that two provinces object to the establishment of courts for the granting o. divorce and hence these divorce bills are before us tonight. None the less I do not think anyone could object if some facilities were provided in one of our federal courts for an aggrieved person to plead his or her case for divorce. We have got to recognize that we have the divorce problem with us, that we have these bills coming beforeparliament regularly at every session, and therefore that there is divorce. If we are going to have divorce let us have it done after a proper and decent investigation.

There is another matter, Mr. Chairman. There is a note of levity sounded when we deal with these bills. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that these bills are all very serious. They are serious for the reason that they have to do with one of the most valuable heritages any nation has, and that is the heritage of the home. Every one of these bills means that a home is being broken. Perhaps it is already broken. I do not know. I just want to say one thing
in reply to the hon. member who was good enough to say some kind words about our committee, and the way it is conducted. He brought up one matter, and I understood him to say the sponsor of the bill should be familiar with the facts. I believe that is the essence of the whole matter. subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO RESULTS OF TORQUAY CONFERENCE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO RESULTS OF TORQUAY CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Trade Agreements
The United States, in addition, has granted numerous important cuts on its entire schedule of tariffs which apply to chemicals, and related products. These include important by-products of the pulp and paper industry, and a number of other products in which our chemical producers are interested. A list of farm products, of definite interest to Canada, has now been added by the United States to the extensive concessions it made in this field at Geneva. Besides Cheddar cheese, the new tariff reductions affect sheep and lambs, frozen blueberries, grapes, hybrid seed corn and mustard seed, amongst others. A substantial reduction was made in the tariff on Canadian whisky. For our coastal fisheries, the concession on canned salmon is accompanied by other concessions which include sardines, fresh mackerel, smoked or kippered herring, clams, fish oil, seal oil and whale oil.
Under the heading of wood and wood products, the important concessions received from the United States on plywoods are supplemented by reduced tariffs on packing boxes and shooks, for which the rate is now to be 3| per cent, and a variety of products manufactured of wood, such as paint brush handles, broom handles and hockey sticks.
Concessions from the United States on metals, and on a wide range of manufactured goods, will be of interest to Canadian manufacturers, who will find that increased opportunities have thus been provided for them to enter the United States market.
Of the sixteen trade agreements concluded by Canada at Torquay, seven were negotiated with important countries of western Europe. Our trade relations with France should be strengthened by the new agreement, which will lead to improved trade for both countries. The negotiations with France were conducted in a most cordial spirit and with the desire on both sides to accomplish the utmost in our common interests. The accession of western Germany has now strengthened the general agreement on tariffs and trade. Her concessions to Canada include farm products, fish, and a number of other commodities. The agreement with Germany is a good omen, that, once the economy of the federal German republic can be stabilized, there will be real opportunities for complementary trade with Canada. In addition, we have now renewed and extended our trade agreements with Italy, with each of the three Scandinavian countries, Norway, Sweden and Denmark, and we have made our first post-war trade agreement with Austria. Belgium remains, from our point of view, one of the best centres of trade on the

continent of Europe. Her absence and the absence of Holland from the list of our new agreements is evidence mainly of the fact that our earlier agreements with the Benelux union left little scope for further improvement at Torquay.
The Department of Trade and Commerce has been unsparing in its efforts to expand and diversify our external markets. This group of new agreements made with important trading countries of western Europe, is illustrative of government policy in regard to exports. Turkey also became a signatory to the general agreement on tariffs and trade and, in addition, we are pleased to have been successful in concluding a tariff agreement with Turkey. Because of currency difficulties in recent years, all of the countries have been unable to buy our goods to the extent that, in other circumstances, they would have wished. Some of their difficulties are being overcome, however, and our trade relations are being strengthened for the future. As a North American country and a dollar country, Canada is anxious to trade with continental Europe, both to buy and to sell. As a member of the North Atlantic treaty organization, and as a country associated with the Organization for European Economic Cooperation, we are aware of the added strength which is given to common aims, by this closer cementing of our commercial ties with continental Europe.
Amongst the Asiatic countries, we concluded four new trade agreements at Torquay, one of these with our commonwealth partner India, and others with the Philippines, Indonesia and Korea. With war existing as a threat, and as a fact, in various parts of the Far East, we have welcomed the efforts made by these countries to participate constructively in the trade and tariffs agreements of the free world. With widespread aspirations for capital investment and development existing as a strong force throughout Asia, we have given our assistance wherever possible and have contributed to the development of reciprocal trade. In our tariff negotiations with the Philippines, we achieved a reduction in the preferential margins granted there to United States goods on a number of items, this being a step forward in overcoming part at least of the discrimination which has existed against Canadian goods. Reduction of preferential margins was obtained on wheat flour, agricultural implements, canned salmon, and a number of other items.
Amongst the Latin American countries, new agreements were concluded with the Dominican republic, Haiti, and Peru. An

excellent agreement was made with the Dominican republic which granted Canada a number of concessions to supplement those we received at Annecy, including fisheries products and a variety of manufactured goods. Our agreement with Haiti is important, from our point of view, in overcoming a disadvantage which has been suffered in that market in the past by our exporters of fish in brine. At Torquay, Canada received mostfavoured-nation treatment from Peru for the first time, an important objective which we have had in mind for a number of years. In addition, we received tariff concessions from Peru on smoked herring, apples, processed milk, canned fruits and vegetables, amongst others. These agreements, added to the ones which have been concluded during the past year with Venezuela, Costa Rica and Ecuador, go far to complete our structure of trade treaties with Latin American countries. Canadian exporters in a number of fields have wanted to expand their connections with Latin American markets and our trade promotion policy has been a vigorous one in that direction. This policy will be continued to the fullest extent possible, even during this period of defence preparations.
In the case of Cuba, I wish to make an announcement of considerable importance. The government of Canada has ensured the purchase on that market, by Canadian refineries or otherwise, of 75,000 short tons of Cuban raw sugar, within each of the calendar years 1951, 1952 and 1953, out of supplies made available by Cuba to the world market. The sugar purchased under this undertaking is to be shipped from Cuban ports, imported into, and not to be re-exported, from Canada. It is to be noted in this connection that purchases under this commitment will normally be made through the agency of private sugar refineries in Canada, and that no subsidization will be involved on the part of the government. A portion, however, of the mostfavoured-nation duty will be remitted to the manufacturers, sufficient in amount to equalize the laid-down cost of Cuban sugar with the laid-down cost of preferential sugars from empire countries.
The sale of non-preferential sugars has reached very low levels in the Canadian market in the recent past. It was never intended that the effect of the preference, extended by Canada on sugar of empire' origin, should be to exclude completely nonpreferential sugars from our market. We have undertaken this new arrangement to ensure that at least some part of our total imports of sugar will be purchased from Cuba during the next three years. We are prepared, furthermore, to enter into similar
Trade Agreements
arrangements with other traditional suppliers of non-preferential sugar to the Canadian market, it being understood that the total imports under all such arrangements will not be in excess of 150,000 short tons of raw sugar per year during each of the next three years. Under present supply conditions, it is not thought that producers of non-preferential sugars, other than Cuba, will be in a position to take full advantage of this arrangement for some time to come.
We have avoided, for the present, any impairment in the sugar preference which has traditionally been extended to the British West Indies and other suppliers of sugar within the commonwealth and empire. Canadian exporters, in recent years in particular, have been in search of external markets beyond those which are encompassed in the British preferential tariff system. The production of our export industries has grown enormously during this period since the second world war, while rigorous import restrictions have been enforced against Canadian goods throughout the British preferential area. These two factors in combination have created the necessity for Canadian exporters to extend their efforts beyond their traditional markets. In recent years, the difficulties we have encountered in the British West Indies have been extreme and have been remedied only in part by the recent relaxations of import controls effected there. It is natural, therefore, that there has been a growing interest in the Cuban market on the part of Canadian exporters, who have, at the same time, retained their traditional desire to trade with the British West Indies to the fullest extent possible.
The Cuban government has now undertaken to revalidate until January 1, 1954, important tariff concessions which were originally granted to Canada at Geneva, including amongst others, codfish, wheat flour and potatoes. This will be of definite interest to our maritime provinces. Cuba has withdrawn four detailed concessions from us which she made at Geneva. None of them has accounted for much trade, and Canada is being compensated by a small reduction in the Cuban duty on codfish.
While the new agreements made at Torquay provide a signal contribution to Canada's external trade policy, by far the most important accomplishment was the prolongation of the Geneva and Annecy schedules of tariff concessions. This has now been arranged for a firm period of three years, until January 1, 1954. Tariff concessions originally made by other countries at Geneva and Annecy were contractually bound only until January 1, 1951, after which

Trade Agreements
they could be withdrawn upon due notice. When it is remembered that the twenty-three countries which participated at Geneva account for three-quarters of total world exports, it is clear how important is this matter of prolongation of the Geneva agreements, both for Canadian trade and for the stability of world trade. Concessions made to Canada at Geneva by the United States alone, covered in some fashion almost ninety-five per cent of total dutiable imports by the United States from Canada. Now these gains have been safeguarded for Canadian exporters for at least the next three years.
An opportunity was provided at Torquay for countries to exercise their right, under article XXVIII of the general agreement on tariffs and trade, to withdraw or modify items in their schedules of tariff concessions, in advance of prolonging these schedules for the next three years. Canada and the United States, and a number of major trading countries, undertook not to withdraw any concessions from one another, in the interest of maintaining their present agreements intact. As it turned out, we have succeeded in keeping to an absolute minimum the number of concessions withdrawn from Canada by other countries and compensation was received in every case. They are described in the information which is being made available to the press.
A good deal of attention has already been given to the fact that new agreements were not concluded at Torquay between the United States on the one side and the other commonwealth countries on the other. From the Canadian point of view, it is a matter of regret that these countries failed, at Torquay, to add to the substantial body of tariff concession which they made to one another at the earlier negotiations. It is to be emphasized at the same time, however, that all these countries still continue as full members of the general agreement on tariffs and trade. Their trade agreements with one another, which have existed under the general agreement on tariffs and trade since 1947, are now carried forward virtually intact. I do not wish to intervene in any way in a matter for which the public explanation must come from the governments directly concerned. At the same time, it should be explained, for the benefit of hon. members, that the existing agreements between the United States and the commonwealth countries, other than ourselves, have not been impaired. What these countries have failed to gain is nothing more than the benefits
[Mr. Howe.l
which might otherwise have accrued from Torquay by reason of additions to their present agreements.
Before concluding this statement I should like to pay tribute to the team of officials which conducted the tariff negotiations on behalf of the Canadian government at Torquay. Small in number, the Canadian delegation carried on exacting and complicated discussions over a long period of months. I should like to pay special tribute to Mr. Hector McKinnon, who headed the group which carried on the tariff negotiations. The other members were:
C. M. Isbister, Department of Trade and Commerce; W. J. Callaghan, Department of Finance; A. E. Richards, Department of Agriculture; J. P. C. Gauthier, Department of Trade and Commerce; A. L. Neal, Department of Trade and Commerce; B. G. Barrow, Department of Trade and Commerce; H. V. Jarrett, Department of Trade and Commerce;
S.	S. Reisman, Department of Finance; and H. H. Wright, Department of External Affairs. From the Canadian point of view, Torquay succeeded in deepening and widening the channels of our export trade. The benefits of the new agreements will begin to accrue in the near future and their long-run importance is even greater. Taking into account the new countries which joined in the general agreement on tariffs and trade at Torquay, the total trade of GATT countries now accounts for about eighty-five per cent of the trade of the free world. This has been a great accomplishment of international organization during the past five years, and Canada has had a leading part in it. Whatever the future is to be, Canada and Canadian exporters have been well served by what has now been accomplished at Torquay.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO RESULTS OF TORQUAY CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add a few words to the remarks of my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), particularly as to the effect of the Torquay agreements on the Canadian customs tariff. In this connection I shall table at the conclusion of my statement the Canadian tariff schedule V which contains all the tariff reductions and bindings which were granted by Canada in the course of the Torquay conference. Copies will be available to all members of parliament tomorrow morning.
I do not have to remind members of the house that tariff negotiations are essentially a matter of bargaining, of give and take, in which countries agree to reduce their tariffs on some products in return for concessions on products in the other countries' tariff so

that trade may expand to the mutual advantage of all concerned. In this broad international effort to reduce barriers to trade in the interests of our common prosperity, Canada has continued to play a leading role which is appropriate to our position as the third largest trading nation in the world.
I would like to take a moment to explain schedule V of the Torquay agreement, the significance of the tariff items and the rates expressed in it. The first and most important stage in the Torquay negotiations was the conclusion of separate agreements among pairs of participating countries. Altogether 147 such two-sided agreements were reached between the countries participating. Canada completed successful agreements with sixteen of these countries. As my colleague has already said, in these agreements Canada undertook not to raise for a period of three years its customs duties on the items specified in schedule V beyond the maximum rates stated therein. In return, of course, other countries gave corresponding undertakings in their tariff as explained by my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In some cases the rates shown in schedule V involve reductions from existing duties, while in other cases they represent bindings of existing rates against increase. There is a similar schedule of maximum rates of duty for each of the countries which took part in the negotiations, bound for a similar period of three years. Under the most-favourednation principle, all the concessions which Canada made are automatically extended to all the members of the group regardless of whether or not they negotiated directly with Canada. Similarly, the concessions of the other countries are automatically extended to Canada.
The Canadian schedule V is divided into two parts. Part I includes all the undertakings with respect to those countries to whom we grant most-favoured-nation treatment, and part II covers the undertakings made to those countries to whom we grant the preferential tariff. The concessions made in the most-favoured-nations part cover 397 items or subitems, of which 261 are reductions and 136 are bindings of existing rates. Canada's total imports from all countries under the 261 items or subitems on which the mcst-favoured-nations rate was reduced at Torquay amounted to about $390 million in 1949.
Part II of the Canadian schedule contains some seventy-five items or subitems on which reductions were made in the preferential tariff. These reductions should mean
Trade Agreements
increased opportunities for the United Kingdom and other commonwealth countries to export to the Canadian market.
I feel I should say a further word about the effect of Torquay on Canada's position with respect to the commonwealth preferential system, because I am afraid there has been some misunderstanding about this matter. To begin with, I would like to make quite clear to members of the house the conditions under which the Torquay negotiations were undertaken and conducted.
Under the rules governing the tariff conference at Torquay, as well as the previous conferences at Geneva and Annecy, it was provided that the reduction of preferences was to be one of the matters subject to negotiation. These rules state clearly that "prior international obligations shall not be invoked to frustrate negotiations with respect to preferences, it being understood that agreements which result from such negotiations and which conflict with such obligations shall not require the modification or termination of such obligations except with the consent of the parties to such obligations".
The rules go on to say that "no participating government shall be required to grant unilateral concessions or to grant concessions to other governments without receiving adequate concessions in return". It was clearly understood that no preferences need be reduced nor any tariff concessions granted except in return for reciprocal and mutually advantageous concessions, and it was up to each country to decide what constituted a satisfactory agreement from its own point of view.
These rules governing the conduct of the Torquay negotiations with respect to preferences were accepted by all the participating countries, including all the commonwealth countries. Indeed, as a practical matter, it would be quite impossible for Canada or the other commonwealth countries to negotiate successful and mutually advantageous agreements with countries outside the preferential system unless they were prepared to negotiate on this basis. This is so because the Canadian tariff and the tariffs of the other commonwealth countries provide for a preferential treatment over pretty well the whole range of their tariffs.
This government has never taken a rigid or doctrinaire position on the matter of preferences either with respect to their retention or modification. For that matter, as members of the house will recall, Canada took

Trade Agreements
the lead many years ago in granting preferential treatment to commonwealth countries. As hon. members know, we have used the device of commonwealth preferences as a device for expanding trade. We have never regarded it as a device for restricting trade.
Our objective has always been to expand trade on as wide a basis as possible. Indeed, this is the only way in which we can find adequate outlets for the products of our expanding economy. For this reason, while the government continues to attach a high importance to the development of intercommonwealth trade, it has never allowed our preferential arrangements to prevent us from taking advantage of new opportunities for expanding Canada's trade. In order to find adequate outlets for the products of the different regions and industries of this country, we must take advantage of such opportunities.
In the course of the Torquay tariff negotiations, as was the case at Geneva and Annecy, in order to obtain valuable concessions from the United States, western Europe and other non-commonwealth countries, we agreed to the modification and in some cases to the elimination of certain margins of preference. Having said this, I want to make it clear that Canada has not abandoned commonwealth preferences. These preferences have been modified in successive negotiations of trade agreements since 1935, but they are still an important part of our tariff structure.
I do not intend to take the time at this late hour to go into detail on the several hundred items contained in schedule V. This is being done in the information being released to the press this evening. I would like to say, however, that in making tariff reductions we have in many instances selected products which would, in these times of inflation and high prices, help to ease the burden for the Canadian consumer. In that connection, Canadian housewives will be interested in the reduction of the customs duty on such items as grapefruit juice, bananas, salt pork and beef, cocoa beans, walnuts, canned fish, and household matches. Of benefit to the consumer generally are the reductions on rubber tires, rubber hose, household furniture, hand tools, certain electrical appliances, and cutlery.
We have also tried to keep in mind the needs of Canadian industry and have made a number of important reductions in equipment, parts, and raw materials, which should contribute in a real way to lower costs of production-machinery of all kinds and parts thereof, motor vehicle parts, off-highway

trucks, rayon yarn and rayon fabric, just to mention a few of the important products affected.
Of special interest to agriculture are the reductions on insecticides, baling wire, seed and grain cleaning machines, and electric motors for attachment to farm implements.
I know that members will be interested in knowing how soon the tariff reductions made by Canada will come into force. The concessions exchanged among Canada, the United States, France and a number of other countries will come into effect on June 6. These, I believe, cover by far the largest part of schedule V. The exact date on which Canada will extend concessions negotiated with the other countries depends on when they are in a position to take similar action. It is expected that all the Torquay concessions will be in force not later than November 20.
As in the case of the previous agreements, the tariff changes contained in schedule V will be brought into effect under the authority of section 11 of the customs tariff.
