subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO RESULTS OF TORQUAY CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it was very comforting and reassuring to hear the minister say, in closing his address this afternoon, that Canada is not at war. I am sorry he did not have the opportunity of seeing the five o'clock edition of this afternoon's Journal before making that remark. I have it before me, and these are the headlines: "Big force of Russian planes massed near Korea-Marshall." And directly underneath that: "Atomic fire rain no dream, says Martin, pleading for fighting Canadian spirit. 'Whip up fury against Soviet threat'." Another headline: "Red Japs not far from Japan." Then on the other side of the page: "British unit honoured on epic stand."

It seems to me the time has come to do away with these soft speeches, to let the people of Canada know we are in a very precarious position at the present time, and to give the people a little better knowledge of the enemy we are fighting. We may not be at war, but we are in a war, and in it right up to our necks. The last sentence in the white paper tabled by the minister has this to say:
We must be prepared to meet either the challenge of general war or the continuation of effort over a generation.
That does not sound very much as though we were not at war. Probably we do not realize just how true that statement is. There can be no peace for any free country until the scourge of communism is wiped off the face of the earth. Let us not forget that at any time. We have been warned time and again by the various communist leaders that they intend to conquer the world and will let nothing stop them. In 1847 Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, in drawing up their communist manifesto, had this to say:
The communists declare that their ends can be attained only by the forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions.
In 1920 Lenin had this to say:
It is necessary to use any ruse, evasion, cunning, unlawful methods, concealment of the truth. As long as capitalism and socialism exist we cannot live in peace.
That is the enemy we are fighting today, not only on the field of battle but in the cold war. The only way we can overcome communism is either by defeating it in an all-out war or by keeping our forces built up to such an extent that the communist forces will not dare attack the western powers, and keeping them that way until some internal revolution upsets the communist government in Russia. Those are the only two alternatives.
We cannot win this war by arms alone. We have to fight by means of propaganda and by feeding and clothing the undernourished peoples of the world. The Colombo plan as it is drafted is very commendable, but it is about twenty years too late. Now we have lost most of the Orient, because the only policy we had there in the early days [DOT] was to get out of it everything we could and put back as little as we could get away with.
As far as the arms race is concerned, if we can believe press reports that we see from day to day Russia is far ahead, so far that it is going to take us a long time to catch up at the rate we are going, and maybe we will not have that time. I believe it was the hon. member for Acadia who on February 15 of this year placed on Hansard a quotation from the June, 1950, issue of
Supply-National Defence United Nations World, which said Russia had 30 million trained men at her disposal. That was a year ago; we can draw our own conclusions as to what she may have today. On February 14 I placed on Hansard a quotation which said Russia was producing 400 jet planes a month. That same quotation said that the United States was only producing 250 planes per month of all types. Speaking of plane production, Mr. Chairman, only recently a number of members visited the Canadair plant in Montreal, and saw the possibility of producing numerous planes there. At that time some of us were told that the company was producing something like ten F-86 Sabres per month. If they were given the materials and manpower, they could produce ten per day. On page 6 of this white paper the minister says:
The reason that radar and fighter defence is not already fully operational is that the radar, the type of communications selected and the aircraft-the F-86E Sabre and the CF-100 Canuck-have only been recently developed and have not yet been produced in the numbers required. As fast as aircraft can be produced, regular and auxiliary fighter squadrons will be manned and equipped to war strength. In the interim, the R.C.A.F. has mobile radar sets and Vampire and Mustang fighters.
If it is only a case of waiting for production of these types of planes, let us give them the men and materials and let them produce the planes. Then we can bring our forces up to, strength. In a time like this nothing should stand in the way of defence production. We saw an exhibition put on by the CF-100 over a year ago. If all the prophecies and statements made regarding that particular aircraft are true, we certainly should have more than one in the air at this time. I believe we had two, but one of them crashed. After a year we have exactly one of the type of aircraft that Canada claims is the best of its kind in the world. We cannot spend all of our time experimenting. We have to make a start somewhere. We have these two types of planes, we have the means to produce them, so let us go ahead and produce them.
Over a year and a half ago. I asked the minister about anti-submarine vessels. He said there was a new type under consideration, and construction would start shortly. I believe the keel was laid in January, 1950- the minister can correct me if I am wrong. These ships, as well as these planes, have to be produced as quickly as possible. We cannot waste time, so let us get at it. This is a matter which concerns our very existence. It is not a game. It cannot be a game, because the other fellows will not play fair. If we are going to lick them, we will have to get to work and get into production. Korea is only the opening battle in this war. We have no reason to believe it will not spread

Supply-National Defence until it is a global conflict. We must build up our forces and our armaments now. Canada has a three-year program under way, and that is fine. The program should have been started three years ago, because we do not know whether it will be a matter of weeks before we are actually engaged in battle either here or in Europe or some place else.
Speaking of being engaged in a battle, I do not believe the minister or anyone else in this house could convince those boys in the foxholes in Korea that we are not in a war. If they are willing to give us all they have, surely the least we can do is to gear ourselves to maximum production to give them everything we can to help them along. We have no reason to believe that this war, when and if it breaks out, is going to be in Europe or in Asia or in Africa, the middle east or anywhere else. It may be right here. We also have no reason to believe that the Russians have not at this time, somewhere in the north, set up camouflaged rocket installations. It is not entirely beyond the realm of possibility.

That is what I said, Mr. Chairman, so far as we know; that is the point I am making. We have no reason to believe they could not send suicide bombing missions, and if they did central Canada would make a beautiful target. Practically nine-tenths of our industry is consolidated in that one little spot. We need a further decentralization of our defence industries, so that if the one area should be knocked out we could still carry on. We have all the power- coal, water and gas that is needed in the province of Alberta. I am inviting those industries to come out there. Speaking for my own constituency, they could move in
tMr. Thomas.]

next door to the Leduc oil field any time they wish, and they will be welcome.
According to the minister's statement the reserves are going to be used as the basis for recruiting for the 27th brigade. I would suggest that the minister start looking around now for ways and means of recruiting men in the reserve forces to bring them up to strength. A strong reserve force in Canada could well mean life or death to Canadian civilization.
One more point, Mr. Chairman, and that is the paying of income tax by the members of the special force. No man who volunteers to face death to fight for the things we believe are right should be asked to pay taxes to help equip himself. It should be enough that these men are willing to fight our battle for us, suffer untold misery and sometimes death. They should not be asked to dig into that pittance which is their pay to give some of it back to the government. We are fighting a war, Mr. Chairman, perhaps the most important war that has ever been fought in history. Let us not go about it haphazardly. Let us fight this war with every ounce of our resources and every means at our disposal. But let us fight this war according to the highest ideals inherent in the Christian democracy that we represent.

subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO RESULTS OF TORQUAY CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in speaking of defence, one is mindful of the problem facing this country, with its large area and scattered population. We cannot by any stretch of the imagination adequately defend all parts of this country. Our defence is therefore interwoven with the United States in defending the North American continent, and that policy is sound common sense.
We have heard something of invasion by Russia by way of Alaska, and by paratroopers in our northwest and British Columbia. While nothing is impossible in modern war, my opinion, for what it is worth, is that this natural fear by those who live in that part of Canada is not fully justified.
The main principles of war never change; the methods by which war is conducted do change and change rapidly in modern times. One of the first principles of waging successful war is to destroy the war-making potential of the enemy. The second principle is to concentrate overwhelming power at the correct time and place, and to strike with all the force at one's command to gain a favourable decision. To carry these principles out by invading Alaska or our Northwest Territories would in no way destroy our warmaking potential nor would it have any decisive effect on winning a war on this continent by invasion.

You have only to look at this vast territory, thinly populated, with its tough terrain and climate, readily to see how formidable such a task is. Besides, the enemy would be fighting at the end of a long line of communications. To feed and maintain troops with all the equipment a modern army requires to wage successful war under such circumstances would be hazardous in the extreme. Especially is this so in the face of two of the most powerful military countries in the world, Canada and the United States, who could concentrate their great power much quicker and on shorter lines of communication. In the last war, Japan tried something of the sort when she landed troops in the Aleutian islands, but as soon as we concentrated against her, and after some small-scale fighting, she cleared out. Nuisance raids on a small or somewhat larger scale could be attempted, but they would have little or no effect on winning a war and their value to an enemy would be only to draw our attention away from the main threat and to force us to concentrate more troops than necessary for the defence of this territory.
A third world war means a global war. In such an event our main danger would be on the Atlantic. During the last two world wars we won the battle of the Atlantic by only a very small margin; and many times it was touch and go with us. The history of this struggle during the last war clearly shows that we won only just in time. If the new modern German submarine with the schnorkel device had made its appearance sooner and in quantity, it would have gone very hard with us indeed.
This is the menace we face today. From the best available information we find that Russia has large numbers of those modern submarines in commission; and if our countermeasures are not equal to the task of dealing with them, we can look forward with great anxiety to our shipping on the Atlantic. I do not wish to say more about this matter at this time, nor do I think it advisable. However, I do think the attention of the committee should be drawn to it.
We have been obliged to learn, abruptly and rather brutally, that one cannot beat something with nothing. Noble gestures, honest purposes and good resolutions will not of themselves stop a military invasion. Planes and tanks are required to stop planes and tanks.
In that connection, we have also had forced upon us the realization that appropriations in parliament do not equal arms in the field. We may eventually learn to speak of "arms aid" not in terms of so many millions appropriated, but in terms of so many weapons
Supply-National Defence put in the hands of troops and of so many men trained and ready to act.
We also have learned that we have been and are being faced by an implacable and entirely unscrupulous enemy. The free people of the world will be attacked when and how that enemy chooses. There is no reliance to be placed upon honeyed words or "peace petitions." There is no peace and there is no chance of achieving it except by matching strength with strength.
General Eisenhower speaking on this subject last fall stated to the American people as follows:	"Get tough with yourselves to
assure victory in this bitter, and probably prolonged struggle."
All lesser considerations must wait, he said; we cannot tolerate politics as usual any more than we can tolerate business as usual.
"The die is cast in Asia, but we are in no limited conflict. Free Europe ... is a tempting target for predatory military force." And he warned that Soviet planners contemplate the same fate for all the world, including the United States of America and Canada, as Russia has imposed on its satellite countries.
We in Newfoundland are the cornerstone of North Atlantic defence. That is the reason for so many United States naval, land and air bases in our province. One look at the map of North America can demonstrate this. I find that at present only one ship of the Royal Canadian Navy is permanently stationed in Newfoundland, and that is used chiefly for training purposes. I really think this is not sufficient at this time and would suggest for the consideration of the naval authorities that at least one additional ship, either a destroyer or frigate, should be permanently based in Newfoundland waters. This, I believe, is necessary and would stimulate recruiting and training for our naval forces. The Royal Navy had such a ship stationed at St. John's for many years with excellent results. I am convinced we can do likewise with even better results.
I should like at this time to speak briefly about our forces in Korea. This parliament called them to the colours; this House of Commons sent them overseas. During this session very little has been said about our boys fighting in this distant land. Very little has been published lately by the press of this country about how our forces are faring. Without in any way criticizing anybody, I do think everybody has been somewhat negligent in this matter. We have a duty to those men of ours, namely to see to it that they are ever in our thoughts, that we take a great interest in their welfare and that we are

Supply-National Defence solidly behind them in all they do. They are fighting as much for freedom and democracy in Korea as if they were fighting on the soil of Canada. There are fighting for each and every one of us and they must be made to feel that the members of this parliament feel that way about them. In no sense must they even think that they are a long way from home and out of our thoughts. We can and must do all that is possible to stimulate their fighting spirit and to help to maintain their morale which is so essential.
In this respect I suggest for the consideration of the minister that a small party of members of the house in the not too distant future proceed to Korea and visit all our forces there, conveying our interest and good wishes to all ranks. They are the flower of our youth and the pride of the nation. To us they represent Canada; to us they are Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, Canada's defence policy or defence program, perhaps I should say, for the next three years, was put before parliament by the minister on February 5; and the white paper which we received yesterday is to a large extent a reiteration of what he said at that time. I welcome the minister's statement for several reasons. To begin with, I welcome it because it was the first statement of defence policy worthy of the name which we have had in the past several years. As to the program, the main emphasis in it is on the development of air power. With that emphasis I think the majority of the members of this committee and of the people of Canada will agree, particularly at this time. There are several reasons for that. This country is particularly well adapted to the development of an air force, and the development of a force of that sort takes a considerable length of time. For that reason alone I was glad to see that the government had decided this year to put a very considerable amount of money into new aircraft, the building of new fields and things of that kind.
With the objectives of our national defence policy which were stated by the minister on February 5, and set out at page 91 of Hansard, I think most of us are in full agreement. I should like to read them again. They are as follows:
(1)	The Immediate defence of Canada and North America from direct attack;
(2)	The implementation of any undertakings made by Canada under the charter of the United Nations, or under the North Atlantic treaty or other agreement for collective security;
(3)	The organization to build up our strength in a total war.
The mere statement of these objectives, Mr. Chairman, immediately raises the question of how and when they are to be met.


The minister proceeded to tell us about that, and to examine each of these objectives in turn, to some extent.
First, the defence of Canada against direct attack is, of course, and must be our primary concern in any discussion on defence matters. From the point of view of the air, we are under a program to counter the threat of Russian bombing, through the use of a radar screen, backed up by fighter squadrons. I think there is no doubt such a project should be our first line * of defence; but I wonder how effective a defence of this kind we are to have.
The over-all plan for the air force, as stated by the minister, calls for forty squadrons. Of these, eleven fighter squadrons are to be in Europe. A considerable number of the remaining twenty-nine squadrons will be transport, reconnaissance and other aircraft of different types along that line. The question, then, is how many fighter squadrons that will leave for the direct defence of this country against enemy bombing. Furthermore, how many of these fighter squadrons will be regular squadrons which will presumably be ready to go into immediate action, and how many will be auxiliary squadrons which from the very nature of things, cannot be immediately operational at anything like full strength?
These questions of course are on the basis of the three-year plan; and the biggest question of all is this: What have we got at the present time? One hon. member this afternoon brought up this point, and said that a great deal of the talk in connection with defence was based upon what we were going to have two years from now or three years from now when this program is completed. He thought there should be more emphasis on what we have at the present time. I think that is extremely true, and that the minister should give us more information of that kind.
I think there is no question that a large number of people in Canada are very much afraid that at the moment we are almost defenceless against an enemy bombing attack, if it should come next week or the week after. These people are very anxious that such a situation will not continue, and particularly that it will not continue for anything like a year or two years longer.
Then, turning to the army, the minister >
said:
To supplement these air defences the army has a large stock of heavy anti-aircraft guns to be manned by active and reserve force personnel.
Leaving aside what is meant by "a large stock", I know we have not the trained personnel to man these guns, in either the

regular or the reserve army. I have heard nothing from the minister as to how the men required are to be raised and trained. The anti-aircraft defences of this city of Ottawa are typical. It is the responsibility of a reserve anti-aircraft regiment, and I doubt very much whether that regiment could turn out a complete troop of four guns; and if it did turn out that troop of four guns, such a troop would be insufficiently trained to put up an effective defence.
Statements of this kind, which I think are meant to be soothing, actually in my opinion are dangerous. It is no use for the minister to say we have a large number of antiaircraft guns if we have not the personnel trained to man those guns-and I think there is no question that we have not.
The next paragraph in the minister's speech, as it appears at the bottom of page 91, says this:
In addition to attack by air, it might be possible for an enemy to land airborne troops by a surprise attack on an, airfield or by parachute. To meet this possibility the Canadian army has a specially-trained airborne brigade group.
I believe the three infantry battalions of this brigade are now fairly well up to strength. What the exact state of their airborne training is, I do not know. I should hope it would be up to scratch also. Certainly, however, the three battalions have not trained together as a brigade. So far as I know there is no headquarters in being, certainly not one which has trained with the three battalions; and therefore it is not quite correct to speak of this as an airborne brigade. It is not trained as such and as a result it could not operate as such. What we have, actually, is three airborne battalions, and certain other airborne troops. As I say, they are not ready to operate together as an airborne brigade and, more important, from their airborne role point of view, we have not the transport aircraft to carry them. And until we have that brigade trained as a brigade, and particularly until we have the transport aircraft which will make them operative in an airborne role, it is quite misleading to talk of them as a well-trained airborne brigade.
The two matters upon which I have just made comment, from the minister's speech, indicate that apparently reassuring facts quoted by the minister may not be so reassuring when more closely examined.
The reserve army is a very important part of the defence of Canada against direct attack. The minister said very little about it in his
Supply-National Defence speech. In fact, I think there is only one sentence which refers to it when, as reported at the top of page 92, he said:
In support of the regular forces and to take action to prevent sabotage are the reserve forces as well as the R.C.M.P. and other police.
Of course in the event of war breaking out, apart from the police, the reserve army would be the chief means of dealing with saboteurs. That would probably keep them fairly well occupied for some considerable time. However, on the shoulders of the reserve army, too, would rest the major portion of the burden of the immediate defence of this country, so far as the army is concerned. And, along with that, as a third role it must undertake, is the provision of the framework for mobilization.
The question is:	Is the reserve army
strong enough to carry out these tasks? The minister during the past three years has given us optimistic reports on recruiting and training in the reserves, and has tried to give the impression that all was well in. that regard. The report of the conference of defence associations held in the early part of January in this year effectively disposed of all such arguments and stories on the part of the minister. I should like to quote a few excerpts from that to indicate what the men who command the reserve forces, who run the reserve forces, think of their effectiveness. I quote:
The delegates to the conference of defence associations are all civilians, representing a cross section of Canadians from every part of the country. They, and the men they represent, are in large measure responsible for the effectiveness and efficiency of the reserve force. It is to the reserve force that Canada must look for the creation of a national army in time of war.
Year after year, by formal resolution, the conference has brought to the attention of higher authority the need for some action, if the reserve force is to function as it should, and meet the expectations of the Canadian people that the money spent upon it will produce results when the need arises.
And again:
Large sums have been spent on advertising and in other ways to induce men to join the reserve force. To a large extent, such moneys have been wasted. The men have not been and are not coming forward.
The men represented through the conference have exhausted every effort to improve these conditions and have sacrificed time and their own money in such efforts.
The delegates to the conference feel that, since the effectiveness and efficiency of the reserve forces is largely their responsibility, and that of the men they represent, they would be derelict in their duty to the government and to their fellow countrymen if they did not put before that government and the people of Canada their views as to the present state of the reserve force.
It is obvious that the vastly increased expenditure on military matters now contemplated will call for

Supply-National Defence sharply increased' taxes to be paid by Canadians. We feel Canadians are prepared to pay such taxes in view of the issues involved but we do not feel1 that Canadians are prepared to see moneys wasted. It is our considered and unanimous opinion that proper value is not being received for much of the public moneys now being spent on the reserve force.
In spite of the existing shortages of facilities for the reserve force, in many places the strength of units does not absorb present facilities for training by a substantial margin. Far more men could be trained in the reserve force than are presently coming forward.
The turnover of other ranks is such that the vast majority of men who appear from tune to time on the nominal rolls of reserve force units receive no training worthy of the name. They do not stay with the unit long enough. To say that the reserve force is 40,000 strong, and to give the Canadian people the idea that it has 40,000 men who could quickly be ready for action, is a travesty of the facts. There are few, if any, reserve units in Canada that could be ready to function in action under a minimum period of six months. This includes AA and other such units which should be ready for immediate action. The Canadian public, in spite of the moneys spent, cannot look to effective and efficient protection from internal sabotage or external aggression from its reserve force for a considerable period after war breaks out, and the active force is far too small to undertake the full burden of such duties.
I think that is fairly conclusive as to what the situation in the reserve force has been. Since that report was made some three or four months ago there has been no material change in the situation. The question then arises: What does the minister propose to do to make our reserve army efficient and effective? The trouble does not lie with the men in the reserve. They devote a good deal of time and effort to the defence of this country, time that might otherwise be spent in leisurely pursuits. Their devotion to duty deserves the highest praise and I know they have made the greatest possible efforts to make their units efficient and effective.
The trouble is that they have not been able to get the necessary men with whom to build units. The average young man in Canada has not felt that there is any real need for him in the reserve. This lack of any sense of urgency is the responsibility of this government. At any rate, until quite recently, the government itself has shown no sense of urgency whatever in defence matters. On the contrary, we have had soothing assurances of the adequacy of our defence measures. We have had an attitude of no war in our time and business as usual.
I think that attitude has passed away to some extent and considerably more urgency is being shown by the government at the moment than was the case previously. However, it has not so far carried over to the general public from anything that I can see. The government needs to adopt much more

strenuous measures than it has so far in order to get this over to the young men of this country.
The necessity of a strong reserve and the reliance on it to raise men for the regular forces was indicated quite clearly by the minister's announcement of Friday last that the brigade for Europe is to be raised from the reserve units. In my opinion that is probably the only way in Which it could be raised rapidly by voluntary methods. However, what does not seem to be realized and what has not been indicated by anything the minister has said is that this move will weaken the reserve and weaken it quite considerably toy draining away a large number of the most active and enthusiastic officers and men.
The regular army and1 the special brigade for Korea have already done a certain amount of draining away. If, as seems likely, a large proportion of the 27th brigade now being raised comes from the reserve units which have the responsibility for raising companies in that brigade, it will mean that those units will be much weaker than they were before, and we all know they were weak to begin with. This will be a very serious blow to the reserve army from which it will take considerable time to recover.
The reserve army -has been weakened further in some cases by the withdrawing of equipment. I do not know what has been done with that equipment, but probably some went to the regular force units and probably some was sent to Europe. I should like the minister to indicate when that withdrawn equipment will be replaced.
There has been a considerable amount of talk today with regard to standardization, and during the past year or more we have had a number of .statements in regard to this. The hope has been expressed on many occasions that all the North Atlantic treaty nations would adopt the same weapons and we would have a standardization of arms for that entire confederacy. I think that has now become what might be called merely a pious hope and there is no real expectation that a North Atlantic treaty standardization of weapons will take place. There certainly has been little progress, if any, in that regard.
The Canadian government has decided to adopt the United States type of weapons. At this point I am not going to go into the wisdom or unwisdom of that course. The thing is that because of that policy the British type equipment we have is being disposed of. Equipment for two divisions has been sent already to Holland and Belgium

and I believe equipment lor a third division is on the way to Italy, or will shortly be going there. We have had no information in this house, nor has the country had any information as far as I know, that this equipment has been replaced with United States style weapons.
The situation seems to be that we are in a much worse position now as far as weapons for the army are concerned than we were a year ago. A further pertinent question that the minister should answer is: What is the equipment that has been disposed of to be replaced with, and when is that replacement to be made? We cannot be left in a situation where we have got rid of the major portion of our army equipment and have not received or made anything to replace it. As an example of what has happened, our anti-tank units have had their self-propelled guns taken away from them, and so far as I know they have had nothing to replace them. Perhaps they have been given a drawn gun of some sort with which to carry on a little gun drill. They should be told immediately what they will get to replace the self-propelled equipment they have lost and when they will get it. Without their own weapons with which to train, the interest and morale of such units is naturally going to suffer. It is bound to decline.
While standardization of Canadian arms with those of the United States has been decided upon, again very little has been done towards producing such arms in Canada. I was shocked to learn in the public accounts committee that the only standard1 weapon being produced in Canada so far is the 3-inch naval gun. So far as I have been able to determine no tooling up has been done for the production of other American type weapons in this country. The minister has made no statement as to how much United States equipment we have bought, if any. It is a very serious situation for us to be in to have got rid of more than half of our army equipment without anything to replace it, if indeed that is the situation, as I fear it is.
There is another phase of this matter on which I should like to comment briefly. Some of the United States equipment is not as good as the British type we have had. A case in point, which was mentioned by the hon. member for Nanaimo this afternoon, is the Bren gun. So far as I can learn, it is a much more effective and flexible weapon than its nearest American counterpart. I understand that the Bren gun can be modified to use -30 American type ammunition, and I should think it would be wise for us to adopt that course. It would be wise both from the point of view of efficiency and from the point of 80709-181
Supply-National Defence view of economy to convert our Bren guns to American type ammunition rather than scrap them.
The same question arises with respect to field artillery weapons. My experience during the last war was that the 25 pounder was a much better weapon than its counterpart, the United States 105. I do not know whether it would be satisfactory to modify our 25 pounders to use 105 ammunition, but in any event it seems to be the reverse of progress to be getting rid of superior weapons and replacing them with inferior ones. It is one of the phases of defence rearmament on which I think we should have some information.
The cost of our rearmament effort is also a very important consideration. In his speech in New York on March 30 the minister emphasized the matter of economy. At that time he said:
We must decrease the unit cost of defence equipment. Unless you actually see it, it is hard to imagine how defence costs have soared.
He went on to say that this was partly due to the increase in prices and partly due to the extreme complexity of much of our modern equipment. He quoted prices as of February 5. He gave the cost of a radar station, the cost of a jet aircraft, and so on. The minister went on to point out that the attempt to secure perfection militates against producing the merely good. He made other remarks along that line. As a matter of fact I think that has been one of the greatest weaknesses and difficulties in producing large amounts of equipment and getting comparatively large forces together either rapidly or cheaply. I think we have always paid a great deal of attention to the matter of trying to produce what we think are extremely superior weapons, and as a result have not produced those weapons in quantity rapidly. There are many examples of that. Russian artillery compared with our own and that of the United States is a case in point. I believe it is produced for about a quarter of the cost or less. It is lighter and more mobile and is only slightly less accurate.
The Thompson sub-machine gun and the Sten gun, both of which were used by our forces in the last war, are another example.
I do not know what the figures are, but the Sten gun would certainly cost very much less than the Thompson sub-machine gun, probably a quarter as much. It was not nearly as nice looking a weapon. People did not like carrying it around, but when it came to a fight the difference between them so far as effectiveness was concerned was negligible. I certainly think that a great deal of time can be saved in re-equipping our

Supply-National Defence forces by equipping them with weapons such as those of which I have given examples rather than attempting at a very slow rate to turn out something which may be very slightly better, and may in some cases not even be better at all.
Somewhat the same thing applies with respect to the amount of equipment with which troops are supplied that they are forced to carry, and so forth. There have been a considerable number of accounts in United States magazines and newspapers of late iponths concerning how the efficiency of their forces was actually cut down by too much and too heavy equipment as a result of which lives were lost which should not have been lost. Along with that, it was pointed out that there are far too many men in service units of all kinds compared with the number actually fighting. The same thing applies to our own army and other forces.
I have spoken on this general line many times in the house in the past with respect to our own forces. One of my chief criticisms during the past three years has been that our set-up is top-heavy, that the great majority of our personnel were in headquarters and performing administrative jobs, and very few were in fighting units. During the last few months the percentage of people in administrative jobs compared with the percentage in fighting units has of course decreased considerably because of the formation of the special brigade in Korea, and now because of the formation of the new brigade for European service, and also because of recruitment up to strength of the units in our airborne brigade.
The same thing applies to the air force and the navy. However, I think we still have too 'tnany men at headquarters and in administrative jobs. I think we are still much more top-heavy than we should be. At the last session the minister said that efforts were constantly being made to improve this situation. I should like him to tell us what has been done. It is no use for him to quote to us what the percentage of improvement has been. I should like to have some definite information as to how many men have been transferred from administrative jobs to fighting units, and things of that sort. As a matter of fact I have seen some evidence that the situation is worse. I do not mean from a percentage point of view, but there are more people in administrative jobs at headquarters than there were before, and that number is increasing all the time. That impression may be incorrect, but it is certainly true in some places. While I am on the subject of the cost of defence, we know that during the past four years we have voted large sums in this

house for defence, and a very greatly increased amount is being asked for in this year's estimates. At no time has there been any reluctance to provide the money asked for; nor will there be on this occasion, either in this house or, I think, on the part of the people as a whole. There has been, however, and there is very great concern that the money so voted should be well spent, and that value in fighting ability should be obtained for it.
Past experience in this regard has not been good. In the past three years we have not had very much in the way of fighting units in return for the large amounts that have been spent. Part of our job as members of parliament is to see that the money voted is well spent and that efficient and effective fighting forces are produced. We cannot do that sitting in committee of supply as we are at the moment. I think the only way we can do it at all reasonably is by means of a committee on defence. We have asked for such a committee every session during the past several years, and every session the minister has produced a number of what I would call excuses as to why such a committee should not be set up. I think there is no question but that this is the only way a real scrutiny of defence estimates and expenditures can be made by this House of Commons, and I would again urge the minister to set up such a committee.
Manpower still remains the basic problem in our defence effort. The scheme announced by the minister the other day for raising a brigade for service in Europe is more likely to obtain the number of men needed than any other method which could be devised under the voluntary system. If it does not provide the men needed rapidly, then I think we must face the fact that voluntary recruiting has failed. I sincerely hope the number of men required is raised, and I should hope that would be done within two weeks. In any event I am quite sure all Canadians will wait with great interest to see the results of that scheme.
I should like to offer a few more comments in connection with that matter. I have gone over the list of units each of which is to raise a company, battery, squadron or other sub-unit, and I am puzzled by an analysis of this list. The fifteen infantry battalions to raise a company each are perfectly logical. As the minister said this afternoon, that will give us three battalions of five companies each. However, there are six artillery regiments listed, each to raise a battery. That, of course, would give two regiments of artillery. A brigade group only calls for one regiment of artillery, and I wonder if the

minister will tell us what the second regiment that would be provided is to be used for. Most surprising of all, however, is the ten armoured regiments listed. Does this mean it is intended to raise two or three armoured regiments, or what does it mean? It is not even clear whether the brigade group will have an armoured regiment, though the numbers would seem to indicate not. Therefore just reading over the list it is rather hard to understand just why each of the ten armoured regiments is being called upon to produce a unit or sub-unit for this force.
In the minister's speech of February 5 he said the general defence plan for Canada called for the equivalent of one division in the army. Later announcements seemed to add up to considerably more. We will have one brigade group in Korea and one in Europe, with the airborne brigade at home. It has been announced that the overseas brigades are to be rotated with ones from Canada, which would indicate that we would require at least one more brigade unless the airborne brigade is to be used for this rotation job, which would be directly contrary to all statements of policy that have been made in connection with the employment of that brigade. In addition we need the equivalent of another brigade to provide reinforcements for the troops fighting in Korea. The provision of these reinforcements must have first priority in the allocation of army manpower. At one time there was some talk that the third battalions of the regular infantry regiments, which according to the newspapers today are now on their way to Wainwright from Fort Lewis, would be used as the basis of the brigade for Europe. I am very glad that idea has been given up, if it was ever entertained. I sincerely trust that these third battalions will be brought up to strength and kept as reinforcements for our brigade in Korea. The normal wastage there, apart from battle casualties, is likely to be high; and of course we never know what the battle casualties will be.
The number of men to be raised under the scheme just announced, if it is successful, will amount to 250 per company. That will give us quite a few more men than will be required for the European brigade. A normal infantry rifle company is just a little more than half that number. So if the scheme is completely successful it will mean that we will raise nearly twice as many men as will be required for the brigade group in Europe.
I would like the minister to tell us what it is proposed to do with these men. Are they to go into a general reinforcement pool for the whole army? Are they to be held as 80709-1814
Supply-National Defence reinforcements for the European brigade? Or are they really to form the major part of another brigade group for rotation purposes? Certainly in view of the greater number of men involved it is now apparent that the target of 115,000 men for the forces, which was laid down in connection with this program, must be increased. It struck me from the beginning that 115,000 men in the forces was much too small a number for the jobs envisaged for those forces. I think the number should have been at least 150,000 in order to do those jobs effectively. I do not believe the program could be carried on with fewer than that. So I say there seems to be no doubt that the number required under the program, if the minister can get them, will be much more than 115,000, because of the large increase already shown in the army.
The whole question of manpower was mentioned this afternoon in connection with the manpower council. When that council was set up at the beginning of this session many of us expressed the hope that it would be used to make a survey of our manpower resources. It has not met since the initial meeting, and apparently has done nothing along that line. A survey such as it could make would be valuable. However, I think it would1 be insufficient for our needs in allocating men and women for the services, for industry and so on. I think we need a scheme of national registration in this country immediately. At the beginning of this session, about three months ago, I urged that such a step be taken and the need is just that much more urgent now. Three months have been lost during which that registration could have been conducted.
I believe one of the chief difficulties as far as our defence effort is concerned has been the absence of any sense of urgency on the part of the government in regard to defence preparations or any other matters. They seem to feel no urgency in regard to the matter of inflation, any more than they have shown any feeling of urgency as far as defence matters are concerned. As a result of the fact that the government has shown no sense of urgency, no sense of emergency, the general public has been lulled into a false sense of security. I do not think there is any question but that you cannot have a rearmament effort, you cannot have a war effort or a semi-war effort, without a spirit of willingness to meet it on the part of your people. The only action on the part of any members of the government I have ever seen to arouse such a spirit was this action on the part of the Minister of National Health and Welfare to which reference is made in tonight's Journal. I should like to commend
2842	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence him for trying to put some pep into this thing, for trying to arouse some spirit in the people of this country. It quotes the minister as saying we should whip up fury against the Soviet threat.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was very pleased to hear the previous speaker speak so highly of the reserve forces. In my opinion he correctly emphasized the neglect of this force as a potential defence force. I feel that they are neglected and discouraged as civilian soldiers. They lack funds. I happen to have served with them during the last war, and I found that funds were lacking to an extent that the officers always chipped in their pay in order to buy equipment, some comforts and entertainment for the troops. The reserve forces also lack social life because of this lack of funds. I find these troops are usually cramped in old barracks or old drill halls that have not been altered for many years. I believe that is because they are not taken seriously by the Department of National Defence, but are merely treated as a reserve police force.
I mention this because one of the units that has been selected to form the 27th brigade is the unit with which I served during the war, the British Columbia Dragoons. This regiment served overseas with distinction in the last war. I am not going to dwell on this subject at any length, but the regiment has been housed in an old school building transformed to serve as a drill hall. Seven years ago the promise was made that new


plans would be drawn, and the plans were actually drawn, to enlarge the hall to accommodate the modern unit that now occupies it. So far nothing has been done. The lands are available, and the plans are available. I presume out of the $5 billion money could be made available. If this unit is to be properly housed that hall should be enlarged, and modern equipment installed such as toilets, bathrooms and so on. In my opinion it is only fair to give these things to the troops that you expect to volunteer in a hurry. I know they will, and you will get your quota out there. Then, the government should do its share by providing proper quarters for training.
Most of the officers who will be called for service with this new brigade will come from reserve units. The officers in reserve units are usually men employed in the ordinary vocations in the town, in stores, offices and so on. They are promoted from the ranks. On their behalf I would ask the government to pay all the costs of the clothing that officers have to buy on entering active service, or upon being given a commission in the reserve army. Either the clothing should be given to them or an adequate amount of money allowed so that they could buy clothing wherever they wished.
I believe the government should reassure these men, particularly the rank and file, that proper care will be taken of them when their service is completed. Today a lot of men question this fact, and they question it when they read such statements in the press as appeared in the Globe and Mail about a week ago. The article is headed "Korea Veterans Seek Own Route to Civvy Street." It reads:
Korean brigade soldiers discharged this week found that the federal government had made no effort to pave their road back to civvy street.
D.V.A. officials said representations have been made to Ottawa for assistance to the veterans, but no re-establishment action has been authorized. There were no re-establishment credits, educational grants, Veterans Land Act, discharge leave or clothing allowances for men discharged from the UN force. Only unemployment insurance benefits are available and these only to men with over nine months' service-which few men of the brigade can yet claim.
A few medical discharge cases now being "processed out" get their pay, but nothing more.
"If a man declares himself destitute he may get a $30 voucher to obtain clothing, but this is supposed to be deducted from the army pay owing to him," an army spokesman said today.
I am not going to mention that further, but I would say to the minister that if he expects to recruit the full number of men for the armed services, then those men must be given the assurance that they will receive

proper, just and fair treatment on being returned to civilian occupations afterwards.
I am going to deal briefly-I hope to pass on a suggestion or two to the minister-with my own province. I believe the Pacific coast has grown in importance, especially in the event of a possible war. I believe the minister should take certain steps to remove bottlenecks which prevent the free flow of traffic east and west. We in British Columbia are fully conscious of these bottlenecks, but have become so accustomed to them that possibly we do not object. The first problem is the immediate completion of the trans-Canada highway. I believe this has been a long standing need, and the speed with which it is being completed is far from satisfactory. For the sake of civil defence and the needs of war, the minister should see that the trans-Canada highway from Alberta to British Columbia is completed at a very early date.
The other bottleneck which I have always felt should be removed, not only for the war effort but for peacetime as well, is the railway track running on each side of the Fraser river from Kamloops to Vancouver. On one side you have the Canadian National, and on the other side about one hundred or two hundred feet away is the Canadian Pacific. They both run on single lines because there is not the width to allow for double tracks. Any time there is a meet they have to wait, sometimes for hours, to be overtaken on a siding, and there are not many sidings along that route. The result is that both the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway suffer a severe bottleneck by way of slow transportation; whether it is wheat, troops or passengers, it does not matter. My suggestion would be that these two railways get together, either with the aid of the government in some way or at the insistence of the government, and make the Canadian National a one-route railway going east and the Canadian Pacific Railway a one-route railway going west from Kamloops to Vancouver. In that way traffic would be speeded up and long waits for shunting at sidings would be avoided. The value of the railway as a transportation system, between Kamloops and Vancouver, would probably be doubled. I merely pass that idea long.
Another bottleneck that we have, possibly by the very nature of our country, is that with respect to airports. We have possibly two dozen airports in the interior of British Columbia, an area several times larger than the British isles which has as many hundred airfields. We in the interior are independent and some years ago we started building our own airfields; but owing to lack of funds, we were not able to build fields that could be of
Supply-National Defence use during war. We have, however, retained sufficient land so that the present fields could be extended to be of value in case of war. I could mention such places as Grand Forks, Kelowna, Vernon, and Kamloops. They are prepared to extend their airports in order to accommodate military planes.
As to Grand Forks, on their behalf I have already offered the government the full use, by lease, gift or in any other way, of their excellent port. All it needs is a slight extension to make it of first-class strategic importance, as it is close to Trail. Failing the government's taking active steps to do this, I am satisfied that the municipalities concerned are willing to co-operate and that, given a little bit of assistance, they would carry out the work themselves.
To my mind, these ports are important in the interior. They are safe from attack. They are not as vulnerable to enemy bombing and so on as they would be if they were actually on the Pacific coast. I feel that the government should investigate the possibility of having jet planes in the interior; because by jet planes particularly it is only about twenty-five minutes from Vancouver or maybe thirty-five minutes from Victoria. They would be quite safe in the interior in contrast with the danger they would be in from bombing at the coast.
The subject of my talk tonight was not to be that, but I became a bit sidetracked. My intention had been to speak for a short time on civil defence. I believe this subject is neglected too much by those who speak in the House of Commons, by the government and by the municipalities throughout the country. I believe that the public today are confused for want of instruction and authentic information. If you doubt this statement, I would ask you to just go outside in this or any other town and quite casually ask the first civilian you meet:	What would you do in
the event of enemy planes being reported coming in this direction? Just ask that question of any man or woman in Ottawa or in any other town, and you would be astounded at the blank look which you would receive. They have no answer. They are relying on some government or on some authority to be doing the thinking on their behalf.
We have been told that there are instruction schools and committees functioning, and that they have been set up in various parts of Canada. But the fact remains that the average Canadian has not the vaguest idea of what he should do in case of attack, where he should go or what part he should
2844	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence play in that case. The chances are that the people would scatter like frightened rabbits, seeking the deepest burrow.
One can imagine the confusion of the uninstructed population, faced with a disaster of that kind. We who saw active service remember quite well the terror that demoralized the people, especially the children, in Belgium and France, when the enemy advanced; the thousands who trudged weary miles along roads, going nowhere in particular, sleeping where they could under a hedgerow or maybe in a ditch for better protection. This happened to people in Europe who had first-hand knowledge of previous wars and who had been taught to expect such things. What would happen to our people? What would be the fate of Canadians, lacking instruction, lacking experience and lacking leadership, in towns like Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto or Vancouver? There is only one name for it: complete chaos; and complete chaos will be the result unless we take that leadership in giving these people direction immediately and now. It must be done immediately, because the article that I have already read by the Minister of National Health and Welfare would indicate that this danger is serious and urgent. If we have any pep or any fight, do not let us concentrate it all in Korea. Let us use some of it at home and see that we take adequate steps to protect our people.
I understand that General Worthington is doing his best to arouse public opinion; but instead of touring the country from coast to coast I believe that he would be better employed if he were properly established here in Ottawa, with a competent staff to take care of the provincial organization and

to give proper direction. You cannot do that when you wander around the country giving speeches at Rotary clubs and so on. This thing is urgent. It is as necessary to have him here with a proper staff as it is to have a general staff for the army. I should like to quote what General Worthington had to say on May 5, as reported in the Ottawa Journal of May 7:
Major Gen. F. F. Worthington, C.B., M.C., M.M., federal co-ordinator of civil defence, Saturday urged every man and woman in Canada to accept their responsibilities as part of a countrywide civilian force organized to play their part in the event of invasion.
Speaking at V-E day ceremonies at Aylmer on Saturday afternoon, the general said there was no place on this continent which was not subject to invasion. In a future war America would not be protected1 by the barriers of two oceans and an Arctic icecap.
"Today the front line is your own front yard," he said. He warned that the method of warfare now was to smash at the civil population in order to disrupt the home front and the productive capacity of a nation.
Gen. Worthington said the civilian population would need to be trained to know what to do in the event of invasion to minimize the effect on morale and production.
And he went on to ask the branches of the Canadian Legion to take part in this particular work.
